items.title: Reading Section C 仔细阅读 1
items.paperTitle: 2024年12月大学英语四级（模拟节选）
items.passage: When Mark Stevenson became head of a small design company in Bristol, he noticed that his team spent nearly two hours a day in meetings. Most of them were held in a windowless room and, according to Stevenson, half the people were checking their phones. He decided to try something different: walking meetings. Once a week, the eight members of the team leave their desks, walk to a nearby park and discuss one project while they move. Stevenson says the change has been surprisingly effective. People talk more freely outdoors, and because there are no screens, they listen to each other. The meetings also finish on time, since nobody wants to walk for more than forty minutes. Not every topic suits a walk, he admits; confidential financial discussions still take place indoors. But for creative work, he believes the streets and parks of the city are better than any meeting room. Some researchers agree, noting that light exercise increases blood flow to the brain and helps ideas connect.

questions.q: What problem did Mark Stevenson notice about his team's meetings?
options: They were held in a park.
People often checked their phones.
They lasted less than an hour.
Only eight people attended.
questions.explain: 第一段说 Most of them were held in a windowless room and, according to Stevenson, half the people were checking their phones，即他注意到开会时很多人看手机，故选 B。

questions.q: What is one advantage of walking meetings mentioned in the passage?
options: People talk more freely outdoors.
They cost the company nothing.
They help staff finish more projects.
They are held every morning.
questions.explain: 第三段指出 People talk more freely outdoors, and because there are no screens, they listen to each other，故选 A。

questions.q: Why do walking meetings usually finish on time?
options: Participants have to return to their desks.
The park closes in the early afternoon.
Nobody wants to walk for over forty minutes.
The manager sets an alarm.
questions.explain: 文中说 The meetings also finish on time, since nobody wants to walk for more than forty minutes，故选 C。

questions.q: Which kind of discussion is still held indoors?
options: Creative design work.
Confidential financial matters.
Weekly team planning.
Discussions with clients.
questions.explain: 第四段说 confidential financial discussions still take place indoors，即涉及机密的财务讨论仍在室内进行，故选 B。

items.title: Reading Section C 仔细阅读 2
items.paperTitle: 2024年12月大学英语四级（模拟节选）
items.passage: Every Saturday morning, volunteers gather in a community centre in south London to fix broken things. The event is called a repair cafe, and it is part of a movement that began in the Netherlands in 2009 and has since spread to more than thirty countries. Visitors bring lamps, kettles, bicycles and even clothes, and volunteers with practical skills show them how to repair the items rather than throw them away. The service is free, although visitors are encouraged to buy a coffee or leave a small donation. Organizers say the repair cafes have two aims: reducing waste and passing on practical skills that many people have lost. In a typical morning, about twenty items are repaired, and nearly all of them would otherwise have gone into the rubbish. Some visitors simply come for the company. 'You learn something, you meet your neighbours, and you go home with a working toaster,' one volunteer explains.

questions.q: Where did the repair cafe movement begin?
options: In south London.
In the Netherlands.
In thirty countries.
In a bicycle shop.
questions.explain: Passage 2 第一段说 it is part of a movement that began in the Netherlands in 2009，故选 B。

questions.q: What are the two aims of the repair cafes?
options: Selling coffee and collecting donations.
Reducing waste and passing on practical skills.
Repairing goods and reselling them.
Meeting neighbours and opening shops.
questions.explain: Passage 2 明确说 the repair cafes have two aims: reducing waste and passing on practical skills，故选 B。

questions.q: What do we learn about the items repaired at the cafes?
options: Most of them are electrical goods.
Nearly all of them would otherwise have been thrown away.
They are sold to raise money.
They are given to local schools.
questions.explain: Passage 2 说 about twenty items are repaired, and nearly all of them would otherwise have gone into the rubbish，故选 B。

items.title: Reading Section C 仔细阅读 1
items.paperTitle: 大学英语四级标准模拟卷 01
items.passage:
For most of the twentieth century, the university library was a quiet building whose main purpose was to keep books safe. Students came in, found a title in the catalogue, read it at a table and left. The librarian's job was to protect the collection and to make sure that nothing was lost.

That model has changed almost beyond recognition. A modern university library is more likely to be judged by how many students use it than by how many volumes it owns. Many libraries have moved the shelves to make room for group study areas, computer rooms and small studios where students can record videos or practise presentations. Some have opened cafés, and a few even lend equipment such as cameras, laptops and musical instruments.

The change has not been welcomed by everyone. Older academics sometimes complain that a library without silent reading rooms is no longer a library at all, and that students who work in groups distract those who need quiet. Librarians reply that they have simply followed the students.

Surveys at several universities show that most students still use the building, but for a wider range of activities than their parents did. They borrow fewer printed books, yet they ask more questions, attend more workshops and use more online resources. The most successful libraries, according to a recent report, are those that offer both worlds: a silent floor for those who want it, and lively spaces for those who need to work together. The building has not lost its purpose, the report argues; it has gained several. A library that once stored knowledge now helps students to make it, argue with it and present it, which is a harder job and a more interesting one.

questions.q: What was the main purpose of university libraries in the past?
options: To protect books and keep the collection safe.
To provide group study rooms for students.
To lend cameras and laptops.
To offer workshops on research skills.
questions.explain: 第一段说 the university library was a quiet building whose main purpose was to keep books safe，即过去大学图书馆的主要目的是保护藏书的安全，故选 A。

questions.q: What change have many modern university libraries made?
options: They have built more silent reading rooms.
They have replaced some shelves with group study areas.
They have stopped lending printed books.
They have closed the cafés inside them.
questions.explain: 第二段提到 Many libraries have moved the shelves to make room for group study areas, computer rooms and small studios，即把书架移开腾出小组学习区等空间，故选 B。

questions.q: What do some older academics complain about?
options: Libraries are too quiet for group work.
Students borrow too many books.
Silent reading rooms have gone and students distract each other.
Librarians ask too many questions.
questions.explain: 第三段说 Older academics sometimes complain that a library without silent reading rooms is no longer a library at all, and that students who work in groups distract those who need quiet，故选 C。

questions.q: What does the recent report suggest about successful libraries?
options: They should own more printed volumes.
They should keep students quiet at all times.
They should close social spaces during exams.
They should offer both silent and social spaces.
questions.explain: 最后一段引述报告说 the most successful libraries ... offer both worlds: a silent floor for those who want it, and lively spaces for those who need to work together，即兼顾安静与社交空间，故选 D。

items.title: Reading Section C 仔细阅读 2
items.paperTitle: 大学英语四级标准模拟卷 01
items.passage:
Reading has never been easier, yet many people say they read less than they used to. The explanation is not that books have become less interesting, but that attention has become harder to hold. A phone on the desk offers a constant supply of short messages, and each one gives the brain a small reward. In this environment, a novel that takes three pages to describe a single afternoon can feel slow, even boring.

Teachers and researchers who study reading call the alternative deep reading. They mean the kind of reading in which a person follows an argument, notices the writer's tone and pauses over a sentence that seems especially well made. This does not happen automatically; it requires a quiet place, an unhurried mind and, above all, a decision to stay with one text.

Digital devices are not the enemy. Many readers do their deep reading on tablets, and audiobooks have allowed busy people to return to books they would otherwise never open. What matters is whether the reading is planned or merely squeezed into gaps between messages.

A growing number of universities have therefore introduced short courses on reading habits, in which students are asked to keep a record of when, where and how long they read. The results are often surprising. Students discover that thirty minutes of concentration in the morning is worth more than three hours of half-attention, and that the books they remember most are the ones they read slowly. Perhaps the lesson is simply that reading, like any other skill, improves when it is given time.

questions.q: What do researchers mean by deep reading?
options: Following a writer's argument and pausing over sentences.
Reading as many short messages as possible.
Listening to audiobooks while working.
Skimming a book to find facts quickly.
questions.explain: 第二段解释 deep reading 指 a person follows an argument, notices the writer's tone and pauses over a sentence that seems especially well made，故选 A。

questions.q: What is the author's view of digital devices?
options: They have destroyed the habit of reading.
They are not the enemy and can support deep reading.
They should not be used by university students.
They are only useful for short messages.
questions.explain: 第三段明确说 Digital devices are not the enemy，并举出在平板上深读、用有声书重读书本等例子，故选 B。

questions.q: What do students learn from the short courses on reading habits?
options: Reading in the morning is always boring.
Audiobooks are better than printed books.
A short period of full attention is worth more than hours of half-attention.
Books should be read as quickly as possible.
questions.explain: 最后一段说学生发现 thirty minutes of concentration in the morning is worth more than three hours of half-attention，故选 C。

items.title: Reading Section C 仔细阅读 1
items.paperTitle: 大学英语四级标准模拟卷 02
items.passage:
Every new technology that enters education seems to attract the same argument. Supporters say it will help students who are struggling; critics say it will make them lazy. AI tutoring tools are no exception. These programs can answer questions in clear language, explain a grammar point for the tenth time without losing patience, and give a student immediate feedback at midnight. For learners in places where good tutors are expensive or far away, that is a serious advantage. Studies of basic mathematics and language practice suggest that students who use such tools regularly do improve their test scores, especially when the tool is used for short, focused sessions.

The doubts begin elsewhere. A machine can produce a confident answer that is simply wrong, and a student who has not learned to check may accept it. There is also a quieter worry: if a program always supplies the next step, students may never experience the struggle that teaches them how to think. Teachers report that some students now submit work that is grammatically flawless but strangely empty, as if no one had an opinion behind it.

Most experts therefore draw a sensible line. AI can explain, test and remind; it cannot care whether the student understands. The human teacher remains the person who notices a silent pupil, changes the plan halfway through a lesson and asks the question that makes a class think. In that division of labour, the machine is useful only if the teacher is in charge.

questions.q: What advantage of AI tutoring tools is mentioned?
options: They can give immediate feedback at any time.
They replace the need for human teachers.
They are always cheaper than books.
They help students make friends online.
questions.explain: 第一段说 AI 工具 can ... give a student immediate feedback at midnight，即为学生随时提供即时反馈，故选 A。

questions.q: What do the studies of basic mathematics and language practice suggest?
options: Students should use AI for very long sessions.
Regular short sessions with such tools improve test scores.
AI tools are useless for language learning.
Test scores fall when AI tools are used.
questions.explain: 第一段提到 students who use such tools regularly do improve their test scores, especially when the tool is used for short, focused sessions，故选 B。

questions.q: What is the quieter worry mentioned in the passage?
options: Students may become too polite.
AI tools may cost too much money.
Students may never experience the struggle that teaches them to think.
Teachers may lose their jobs immediately.
questions.explain: 第二段说 if a program always supplies the next step, students may never experience the struggle that teaches them how to think，故选 C。

questions.q: What line do most experts draw?
options: AI should replace teachers in large classes.
AI should be used only in mathematics.
AI should be banned from schools.
AI can explain, test and remind, but the teacher must stay in charge.
questions.explain: 末段说 AI can explain, test and remind; it cannot care whether the student understands，并强调 the machine is useful only if the teacher is in charge，故选 D。

items.title: Reading Section C 仔细阅读 2
items.paperTitle: 大学英语四级标准模拟卷 02
items.passage:
Ten years ago, a student who wanted to study had to leave the internet behind. The phone stayed in a bag, the laptop was used for one task at a time, and a long evening of reading was normal. Today the same student may have six tabs open, a group chat buzzing and a video playing in the corner of the screen.

The result is not that young people cannot concentrate, but that they concentrate in shorter bursts. Researchers who watch students studying describe a pattern of rapid switching: a few minutes on the essay, a quick check of messages, back to the essay, then a search for a fact that turns into twenty minutes of reading something unrelated. Each switch feels harmless, yet the cost adds up.

After an interruption, the mind needs time to return to the point where it stopped, and some studies estimate that this recovery takes several minutes.

The good news is that attention can be trained. Experiments in which students put their phones in another room and worked for fixed periods found that they completed tasks faster and remembered more. Many now use simple methods: a timer for twenty-five minutes of work, a notebook for distracting thoughts, and one evening a week without a screen. None of these ideas is new. What is new is that they have to be taught, because the digital world will not switch itself off.

questions.q: How does the author describe the way many students concentrate today?
options: In shorter bursts with rapid switching.
For hours without any interruption.
Only in the morning.
With the help of AI tools.
questions.explain: 第二段说 they concentrate in shorter bursts，并描述 a pattern of rapid switching，故选 A。

questions.q: What is the cost of an interruption according to the passage?
options: It makes the screen brighter.
The mind needs several minutes to return to where it stopped.
It improves memory of the essay.
It saves time in the long run.
questions.explain: 第三段说 After an interruption, the mind needs time to return to the point where it stopped, and some studies estimate that this recovery takes several minutes，故选 B。

questions.q: What did experiments with phones in another room find?
options: Students worked more slowly.
Students forgot what they had read.
Students completed tasks faster and remembered more.
Students refused to work at all.
questions.explain: 第四段说 Experiments ... found that they completed tasks faster and remembered more，故选 C。

items.title: Reading Section C 仔细阅读 1
items.paperTitle: 大学英语四级标准模拟卷 03
items.passage:
Universities are often described as small cities, and like cities they consume a great deal of energy, produce a great deal of waste and own a great many buildings. It is not surprising, therefore, that a growing number of campuses have started to treat sustainability as a practical problem rather than a subject for discussion. The measures they take are rarely dramatic. One university replaced the lights in its library with sensors that switch off when nobody is in the room, which cut electricity use in the building by a fifth. Another began serving smaller portions in its dining halls and charging less for them, and found that food waste fell by almost a third in a year. Some have built cycle lanes between halls and lecture rooms or offered free bus passes to students who choose not to bring a car.

What interests researchers most is not the technology but the way these changes are introduced. Projects that begin with a student society tend to last longer than those announced by the administration, because students keep using them after the official launch. A survey of twelve campuses found that the most successful projects were small, visible and easy to join: a repair workshop, a book swap, a garden behind the science building. Big targets may look impressive in a report, but a student is more likely to change one habit than to rethink an entire lifestyle. That, the researchers conclude, is how change actually starts.

questions.q: What did one university achieve by replacing library lights with sensors?
options: It served smaller meals in the dining hall.
It cut the building's electricity use by a fifth.
It built cycle lanes on campus.
It opened a repair workshop.
questions.explain: 第一段说 One university replaced the lights in its library with sensors ... which cut electricity use in the building by a fifth，故选 B。

questions.q: Why did food waste fall at another university?
options: Students were given free bus passes.
The university built a garden behind the science building.
Dining halls served smaller portions at lower prices.
Students cooked for themselves.
questions.explain: 第一段提到 Another began serving smaller portions in its dining halls and charging less for them, and found that food waste fell by almost a third，故选 C。

questions.q: What does the survey of twelve campuses suggest?
options: Large official targets work best.
Technology is the key to change.
Students ignore projects started by societies.
Small, visible projects that are easy to join are most successful.
questions.explain: 第二段说 A survey of twelve campuses found that the most successful projects were small, visible and easy to join，故选 D。

questions.q: What do the researchers conclude?
options: Change starts when students change one habit at a time.
Students should rethink their whole lifestyle.
Big targets are the only way to succeed.
Campuses should be treated as cities.
questions.explain: 第二段说 a student is more likely to change one habit than to rethink an entire lifestyle. That, the researchers conclude, is how change actually starts，故选 A。

items.title: Reading Section C 仔细阅读 2
items.paperTitle: 大学英语四级标准模拟卷 03
items.passage:
Bike-sharing schemes were once presented as the answer to almost every urban problem. They would reduce traffic, cut pollution, improve public health and fill the gaps between bus stops and homes. In many cities the first months were indeed a success: brightly coloured bicycles appeared on every corner, and people who had not ridden since childhood began cycling to work.

Then came the problems. Bicycles were left in the middle of pavements, thrown into rivers and piled outside railway stations. Companies competing for the same streets put more bicycles on the road than the city could manage. Several councils responded by limiting the number of bikes and requiring operators to remove those that were badly parked. The result has been a quieter, more useful service. Where parking spaces are clearly marked and repairs are quick, shared bikes have become a normal part of city life. Where they are not, the bicycles soon become rubbish.

The lesson seems to be that a vehicle shared by thousands of people needs the same care as a public library: someone must check it, clean it and put it back in the right place. Technology can help, but the bicycle on the pavement is still a human problem.

questions.q: What was expected of bike-sharing schemes?
options: They would replace public libraries.
They would pay for themselves immediately.
They would reduce traffic and pollution and improve health.
They would be used mainly by children.
questions.explain: 第一段说 They would reduce traffic, cut pollution, improve public health and fill the gaps between bus stops and homes，故选 C。

questions.q: What problem appeared after the first months?
options: Bicycles were too expensive to make.
Too few people wanted to cycle.
Cities ran out of buses.
Bicycles were badly parked, thrown into rivers and piled outside stations.
questions.explain: 第二段说 Bicycles were left in the middle of pavements, thrown into rivers and piled outside railway stations，故选 D。

questions.q: What does the author compare a shared bicycle to?
options: A private car.
A public library that needs care.
A railway station.
A competition between companies.
questions.explain: 末段说 a vehicle shared by thousands of people needs the same care as a public library: someone must check it, clean it and put it back in the right place，故选 B。

items.title: Reading Section C 仔细阅读 1
items.paperTitle: 大学英语四级标准模拟卷 04
items.passage:
In 2019, a fire broke out in the roof of Notre-Dame in Paris. Within hours, engineers were able to consult a detailed three-dimensional model of the cathedral that had been built a few years earlier by laser scanning. Every stone, every arch and every piece of timber had been recorded to within a few millimetres. The model did not prevent the fire, but it made the rebuilding far more accurate than anyone would have thought possible.

The example has encouraged museums and heritage sites around the world to digitise their collections. Some use drones to photograph buildings from above, while others carry portable scanners into caves or narrow temples. At Lascaux, researchers have spent decades recording the prehistoric cave paintings at very high resolution, and the images are now used for both research and education.

Digital copies are not only a backup. They allow people to see objects that are too fragile to be displayed. A page from a tenth-century manuscript may be so sensitive to light that it can be shown to the public only once every few years, yet its digital image can be studied by scholars in Beijing, London or Cairo on the same afternoon. Visitors to a museum in a small town can walk through a reconstruction of a palace destroyed six hundred years ago.

Critics warn that a digital copy is not the building itself. Screens may also tempt governments to pay for images rather than for repairs, since a scan is cheaper than a new roof. Supporters accept that risk but reply that recording a site is the first step towards saving it. 'A building that has been properly recorded,' one architect says, 'is a building we can argue for with evidence.'

questions.q: What was the three-dimensional model of Notre-Dame used for?
options: To guide the rebuilding after the fire.
To attract more tourists to the cathedral.
To replace the damaged stonework.
To train young architects in Paris.
questions.explain: 第一段说 The model did not prevent the fire, but it made the rebuilding far more accurate，即模型用于指导重建，故选 A。

questions.q: How are the high-resolution images of the Lascaux cave paintings used?
options: To sell copies to foreign museums.
To replace the paintings inside the caves.
For both research and education.
To keep visitors away from the caves.
questions.explain: 第二段说 the images are now used for both research and education，故选 C。

questions.q: Why are digital images especially useful for fragile objects?
options: They are cheaper than a museum ticket.
They can be studied without putting the objects at risk.
They are always more beautiful than the originals.
They can be printed and sold as souvenirs.
questions.explain: 第三段说 They allow people to see objects that are too fragile to be displayed，并举对光敏感的十世纪手稿为例，说明数字图像可让人研究而不损伤原件，故选 B。

questions.q: What do critics of digitisation worry about?
options: The high cost of training engineers.
Too many visitors to small towns.
The loss of jobs for museum guides.
Money being spent on scans instead of repairs.
questions.explain: 最后一段说 Screens may tempt governments to pay for images rather than for repairs, since a scan is cheaper than a new roof，故选 D。

items.title: Reading Section C 仔细阅读 2
items.paperTitle: 大学英语四级标准模拟卷 04
items.passage:
When Zhou Lan told her parents that she wanted to become a book restorer, they imagined a quiet job in a library. In reality she spends her days in a workshop in Nanjing, bent over a fragile volume with a fine brush, wheat paste and paper of a dozen different weights. One torn sheet may take three hours to mend, and a badly damaged book can keep her busy for a month.

Traditional book repair was once a small trade, passed from master to apprentice inside a few families. For years, young people showed little interest: the pay was low, the work was slow, and success was invisible. The turning point came when a documentary about restorers became unexpectedly popular online. Applications to the national training programme rose from a handful to several hundred, and the average age of the students fell from forty to twenty-six.

Zhou Lan says the appeal is partly the silence. 'Everything around us moves fast,' she explains. 'Here, if you hurry, you tear the paper.' She also enjoys the moment when an object returns to use. Recently she spent five weeks repairing an eighteenth-century dictionary that a village school had owned for two hundred years, and she refused to accept payment from the school.

Not everyone is comfortable with the attention. Some older craftspeople complain that television crews now visit the workshop in search of beautiful pictures rather than asking about technique, and that a short film cannot show the ten years needed to train an eye. Zhou Lan understands the complaint, but she thinks the interest is a beginning. 'People come for the pictures,' she says. 'Some of them stay for the paper.'

questions.q: Why did few young people want to learn book repair in the past?
options: The work was too physically demanding.
The training programme was too short.
The pay was low and progress was invisible.
The materials were impossible to find.
questions.explain: 第二段说 the pay was low, the work was slow, and success was invisible，故选 C。

questions.q: What brought hundreds of new applicants to the training programme?
options: A documentary that became popular online.
A large rise in the salary of restorers.
A new law protecting old books.
An article in a school textbook.
questions.explain: 第二段说 The turning point came when a documentary about restorers became unexpectedly popular online，随后报名人数大增，故选 A。

questions.q: How does Zhou Lan view the sudden public interest in her trade?
options: She thinks short films describe the work accurately.
She regards it as a useful starting point.
She believes it wastes the restorers' time.
She feels that payment should not be discussed.
questions.explain: 最后一段说 she thinks the interest is a beginning，并说 People come for the pictures... Some of them stay for the paper，故选 B。

items.title: Reading Section C 仔细阅读 1
items.paperTitle: 大学英语四级标准模拟卷 05
items.passage:
When universities advertise volunteering, they usually stress what students can do for the community. A growing number of careers advisers are more interested in the opposite question: what the community does for students.

The evidence suggests that this second effect is larger than students expect. A study following two hundred undergraduates over a year found that those who volunteered for two hours a week were more likely to say they could cope with difficult people and unexpected problems. The improvement did not depend on the sort of work they did. Sorting clothes in a charity shop and teaching children to swim produced similar changes, possibly because both require turning up, paying attention and being useful to someone who does not care about your grades.

Employers seem to notice. In a survey of graduate recruiters, more than half said that volunteering was useful evidence of qualities that interviews cannot easily reveal, such as reliability. One recruiter admitted that a student who had run a weekend football club for three years told her more about commitment than any number of prizes.

There is a risk of exaggeration. Students who volunteer mainly to fill a line on their CV often stop after a few weeks, and a single afternoon of painting a wall proves very little. Advisers therefore suggest choosing one organisation and staying with it for a year. They also warn against letting hours push aside sleep, study or paid work, since a student who is exhausted helps nobody.

The most lasting benefit may be quieter than any of these. Volunteers meet people whose lives they would otherwise never enter, and they learn that a community is not managed by officials alone. That lesson is hard to test, which may be why it is so rarely advertised.

questions.q: What are some careers advisers more interested in?
options: What students gain from the community.
How much money volunteering raises.
Why charities refuse student helpers.
Which subjects volunteers should study.
questions.explain: 第一段说 careers advisers are more interested in the opposite question: what the community does for students，即关注学生从社区得到什么，故选 A。

questions.q: What did the study find about the improvement in students?
options: It only appeared in students of medicine.
It disappeared when the volunteering stopped.
It did not depend on the type of work done.
It was greater for those who worked longer hours.
questions.explain: 第二段说 The improvement did not depend on the sort of work they did，并举例说整理旧衣物与教孩子游泳效果相似，故选 C。

questions.q: What did the survey of graduate recruiters show?
options: Most recruiters ignore volunteering completely.
Recruiters prefer students with high grades.
Recruiters doubt whether volunteering is real work.
Over half of them linked volunteering with qualities such as reliability.
questions.explain: 第三段说 more than half said that volunteering was useful evidence of qualities... such as reliability，故选 D。

questions.q: What do advisers warn students against?
options: Choosing more than one organisation.
Letting volunteering push aside sleep and study.
Working with children without training.
Taking part in activities that last a year.
questions.explain: 第四段说 They also warn against letting hours push aside sleep, study or paid work，故选 B；A 恰恰相反，顾问建议只选一家机构。

items.title: Reading Section C 仔细阅读 2
items.paperTitle: 大学英语四级标准模拟卷 05
items.passage:
In many cities, the people who live closest together know least about each other. A recent experiment in three neighbourhoods tried to change that with a very old idea: a list of what neighbours can offer one another.

The project began with a simple questionnaire delivered to eight hundred homes. Residents were asked to write down one skill they would be willing to share, such as repairing a bicycle or filling in a form, and one thing they needed help with. The replies were surprising in two ways. Only about a fifth of the forms came back, yet those who replied offered far more than the organisers had expected. More importantly, the most frequent request was not practical at all: many people asked for company, someone to walk with in the evenings, or a neighbour willing to knock on the door once a week.

The organisers resisted the temptation to build an app. They printed a small booklet instead and asked the manager of the local shop to keep copies behind the counter. Older residents told them that a screen was exactly the thing that had made them feel excluded. A booklet, by contrast, could be read at the bus stop and passed on to a friend.

Two years later the project survives in a modest form: a monthly repair afternoon, a walking group on Tuesdays, and a list of people who will lend a ladder or a drill. The organisers measure success not by the number of services exchanged but by how quickly newcomers are noticed. 'In a good network,' one of them says, 'a new family is invited to something within a month, without anyone being officially asked to do it.'

questions.q: What surprised the organisers about the replies to the questionnaire?
options: Almost every household returned a form.
Very few residents offered any skills.
The most common request was for company.
Residents asked for an app instead of a booklet.
questions.explain: 第二段说 Only about a fifth of the forms came back，与 A 相反；但 the most frequent request was not practical at all: many people asked for company，故选 C。

questions.q: Why did the organisers print a booklet instead of building an app?
options: An app would have cost too much to develop.
The local shop offered to pay for the printing.
A booklet could be updated more easily.
Older residents said screens made them feel excluded.
questions.explain: 第三段说 Older residents told them that a screen was exactly the thing that had made them feel excluded，因此改印小册子，故选 D。

questions.q: How do the organisers judge whether the project is working?
options: By how quickly a new family is invited to something.
By the number of services exchanged each month.
By the number of booklets printed.
By how much money the project raises.
questions.explain: 最后一段说 The organisers measure success not by the number of services exchanged but by how quickly newcomers are noticed，并以 a new family is invited to something within a month 作具体说明，故选 A。

items.title: Reading Section C 仔细阅读 1
items.paperTitle: 大学英语四级标准模拟卷 06
items.passage:
When students go abroad, they usually prepare for language problems. Few prepare for the quieter difficulty of everyday habits.

A month after arriving in Germany, a Chinese student found that she was exhausted every evening, although her classes were no longer than they had been at home. Nothing was wrong with her health. Her energy was going into small decisions: whether to greet a neighbour in the corridor, how long to wait for a bus that might not come, whether the silence of a shared kitchen meant that her flatmates disliked her. Each choice took seconds, but there were hundreds of them a day.

Researchers who study adaptation call this 'cultural fatigue'. It is not a sign of weakness, and it does not mean that the move was a mistake. It appears in students who are doing well academically as well as in those who are homesick. The usual advice, such as making local friends and joining clubs, is sound but incomplete, because it describes the cure without naming the illness.

What seems to help most is routine. Students who keep one or two fixed habits, such as a Saturday morning run or a weekly cooking evening with the same people, report feeling more settled than those who try to be social every night. Predictability saves energy, and energy is exactly what adaptation demands.

The second helpful thing is a sense of humour about mistakes. Students who can laugh when they use the wrong word in a shop recover faster than those who treat every misunderstanding as a personal failure. Nobody speaks a foreign language perfectly in the first month, and the people serving you are usually too busy to remember your mistake five minutes later.

questions.q: What left the Chinese student in Germany exhausted?
options: Making a great many small decisions every day.
Attending classes that were longer than before.
Cooking for her flatmates every evening.
Travelling to the city centre by bus.
questions.explain: 第二段说 Her energy was going into small decisions，并列举问候邻居、等公交等琐事，故 A 正确；文中明确说课时并不比国内长，排除 B。

questions.q: What do researchers say about cultural fatigue?
options: It only affects students who are homesick.
It can affect students who are doing well in their studies.
It usually disappears within the first month.
It shows that the student chose the wrong country.
questions.explain: 第三段说 It appears in students who are doing well academically as well as in those who are homesick，故选 B。

questions.q: Why is the usual advice thought to be incomplete?
options: It costs money that students do not have.
It is too difficult for most students to follow.
It describes the cure without naming the illness.
It only works for outgoing students.
questions.explain: 第三段说 it describes the cure without naming the illness，即只给对策却没有指出问题所在，故选 C。

questions.q: What seems to help students feel more settled?
options: Trying to be social every night.
Learning the language perfectly.
Living with a local family.
Keeping one or two fixed routines.
questions.explain: 第四段说 Students who keep one or two fixed habits... report feeling more settled than those who try to be social every night，故选 D。

items.title: Reading Section C 仔细阅读 2
items.paperTitle: 大学英语四级标准模拟卷 06
items.passage:
For many years, language teaching in schools concentrated on grammar and vocabulary, and a student could pass an examination without ever hearing a real conversation. That has changed, but not everywhere, and the results of the change are worth examining.

Consider the word 'sorry'. A dictionary will tell you that it expresses regret. In practice, a speaker of English may use it to apologise, to ask someone to repeat a sentence, to interrupt a meeting, or to express sympathy. A learner who knows only the dictionary meaning will sound either too formal or strangely cold. Researchers call this kind of knowledge 'pragmatic competence', and they find that it is often missing in students with high test scores.

The good news is that it can be taught. In one experiment, two classes of students at the same level were compared. Both studied the same vocabulary, but one class also watched short recordings of everyday situations and discussed why the speaker chose a particular phrase. After twelve weeks, that class performed much better in a role-play task, even though the grammar test results of the two groups were almost identical.

None of this argues against grammar. Accuracy matters, especially in writing. The argument is about balance: a language is not only a system of rules but also a set of habits used by a community. Learning a language without its culture is like reading a menu without knowing what the dishes taste like.

questions.q: What does the passage say about the word 'sorry'?
options: It is no longer used in everyday English.
Real speakers use it for several different purposes.
It is the hardest word for foreign learners.
It always expresses sincere regret.
questions.explain: 第二段列举了道歉、请人重复、打断会议、表示同情等多种用法，说明实际使用中它承担多种功能，故选 B。

questions.q: What made the difference between the two classes in the experiment?
options: One class had more experienced grammar teachers.
One class studied twice as many new words.
One class watched recordings and discussed the choice of phrases.
One class spent a term studying abroad.
questions.explain: 第三段说 one class also watched short recordings of everyday situations and discussed why the speaker chose a particular phrase，该班在角色扮演中表现更好，故选 C。

questions.q: What is the author's conclusion?
options: Grammar tests should be abolished.
Vocabulary is less important than it used to be.
Students should read restaurant menus in English.
Language and culture should be learned together.
questions.explain: 最后一段说 a language is not only a system of rules but also a set of habits used by a community，并以看菜单作比，说明语言与文化应一起学，故选 D。

items.title: Reading Section C 仔细阅读 1
items.paperTitle: 大学英语四级标准模拟卷 07
items.passage:
Every spring, thousands of students compete for summer internships, and the pressure is easy to understand. A recent survey of graduates found that those who had completed at least one internship received more job offers than those who had none. But the same survey produced a more interesting result: the length of the internship mattered less than the quality of the feedback the students received.

This finding challenges a common assumption. Many students believe that simply adding a famous company's name to their CV is enough. In practice, interviewers often ask what the candidate actually did. A student who spent three months photocopying documents in a large firm may have less to say than one who spent six weeks in a small studio where the manager explained every decision.

The nature of the work matters too. Tasks that require judgement, such as writing a short report, contacting clients or solving a practical problem, teach skills that cannot be learned from a textbook. By contrast, repetitive tasks may look impressive on paper but leave little to discuss in an interview.

There is also the question of payment. Unpaid internships are often criticised because they favour students whose families can support them. Some employers have responded by offering a modest allowance and travel costs, and a few universities now fund summer placements for students from lower-income backgrounds.

The lesson for students is clear. Before accepting an internship, ask what you will be doing, who will supervise you and whether anyone will comment on your work. A famous logo may open a door, but it is the experience behind the door that employers actually value.

questions.q: What did the survey find mattered most about an internship?
options: How long it lasted.
The reputation of the company.
The salary that was paid.
The quality of feedback the student received.
questions.explain: Passage 1 第一段末尾明确说 the length of the internship mattered less than the quality of the feedback the students received，即反馈质量最重要，故选 D。

questions.q: Why might a small studio offer a better internship than a large firm?
options: It usually pays more money.
The manager explains every decision.
The work is much easier.
It lasts much longer.
questions.explain: 第二段举例说，在小工作室实习的学生有 the manager explained every decision，因而在面试中有更多可谈的内容，故选 B。

questions.q: What kind of tasks does the author value most?
options: Tasks that require judgement.
Repetitive paperwork.
Tasks done straight from a textbook.
Photocopying documents.
questions.explain: 第三段指出 Tasks that require judgement ... teach skills that cannot be learned from a textbook，而重复性工作虽好看却无话可谈，故选 A。

questions.q: Why are unpaid internships often criticised?
options: They last too long.
They offer no training at all.
They favour students from wealthier families.
They are against the law.
questions.explain: 第四段说 Unpaid internships are often criticised because they favour students whose families can support them，即对家庭条件好的学生更有利，故选 C。

items.title: Reading Section C 仔细阅读 2
items.paperTitle: 大学英语四级标准模拟卷 07
items.passage:
Li Na delivers food on an electric bike in a large city in eastern China. She chooses her own hours, works for three different platforms, and earns roughly what she did in her previous office job. I do not have a manager watching me, she says. But if I am ill, nobody pays me, and if the app changes its rules, I cannot argue.

Li Na is one of millions of young people in the growing gig economy, where work is organised through apps and paid by the task rather than by the month. Supporters describe it as freedom: students can earn between lectures, parents can work around childcare, and retired people can take on a few hours a week. For people who find fixed schedules difficult, this flexibility is genuinely valuable.

The disadvantages, however, are also real. Gig workers usually have no paid holiday, no sick leave and no pension contributions from an employer. Their income changes with demand, weather and the decisions of the platforms. When a company alters its payment rules overnight, workers have little power to negotiate, because they are not employees in the legal sense.

Some governments are now experimenting with a middle category that would give gig workers basic protections while keeping their flexibility. Others are leaving the question to the platforms. Either way, the debate is no longer about whether the gig economy should exist, but about how the people in it should be treated.

Young people entering this world need more than a smartphone. They need to understand how their pay is calculated, keep records of their earnings, and think about what happens when they are forty rather than twenty-five. Flexibility is a benefit only if it is chosen with open eyes.

questions.q: What does Li Na like about her work?
options: It pays more than her office job.
It offers sick pay.
She has a manager to guide her.
She chooses her own hours.
questions.explain: Passage 2 开头说 She chooses her own hours，并引用她的话 I do not have a manager watching me，说明她喜欢自己安排时间，故选 D。

questions.q: What is one advantage of gig work mentioned in the passage?
options: It fits around other responsibilities.
It guarantees a monthly income.
It provides a pension.
It offers paid holidays.
questions.explain: 第二段说学生可以在课间挣钱、父母可兼顾照看孩子，For people who find fixed schedules difficult, this flexibility is genuinely valuable，故选 A。

questions.q: What is the main concern about gig workers?
options: They earn too much money.
They work too few hours.
They lack basic protections.
They are unable to use apps.
questions.explain: 第三段列举他们通常没有带薪假期、病假和雇主缴纳的养老金，且平台改规则时难以协商，核心问题是缺乏基本保障，故选 C。

items.title: Reading Section C 仔细阅读 1
items.paperTitle: 大学英语四级标准模拟卷 08
items.passage:
Students often treat sleep as the first thing to cut when exams approach. A week of late nights seems a small price to pay for extra revision. Research on memory, however, suggests that this bargain is a poor one: the hours lost at night cannot simply be replaced by hours spent with a textbook.

The reason lies in what happens after learning. When we first take in new information, the memory is fragile. During sleep, and especially during deep sleep in the first half of the night, the brain replays and reorganises what it has taken in, linking new material to what we already know. Cut that sleep short and the links are weaker. In one experiment, students who learned a list of words and then slept for eight hours remembered far more the next morning than those who stayed awake and revised for the same length of time.

There is a second effect, less obvious but just as important. Tired students find it harder to concentrate and are more easily distracted by their phones. They may sit at a desk for three hours and still absorb very little. Their teachers notice the difference before they do: the same student who was quick and curious in October becomes slow and quiet in December.

The practical advice from researchers is unglamorous. Keep a regular bedtime, avoid caffeine after the early afternoon, and put screens away before going to bed. If a deadline forces a late night, try to recover with a short nap the next day rather than with more coffee. Sleep, they argue, is not time taken away from study. It is part of study.

questions.q: What do many students do when exams approach?
options: They cut back on sleep.
They stop revising altogether.
They sleep more than usual.
They change their diet.
questions.explain: Passage 1 开头说 Students often treat sleep as the first thing to cut when exams approach，即考试临近时学生最先削减睡眠，故选 A。

questions.q: What happens during deep sleep according to the passage?
options: The brain rests completely.
New words are forgotten.
Students become distracted.
Memories are reorganised and linked.
questions.explain: 第二段说 the brain replays and reorganises what it has taken in, linking new material to what we already know，故选 D。

questions.q: What did the experiment with the word list show?
options: Revising all night is effective.
Students need less sleep than adults.
Those who slept remembered more.
All students remembered the same amount.
questions.explain: 实验发现学完单词后睡八小时的学生，第二天记住的内容远多于同样时长保持清醒复习的学生，故选 C。

questions.q: What does the author suggest for a forced late night?
options: Drinking more coffee.
Taking a short nap the next day.
Sleeping late at weekends.
Skipping breakfast.
questions.explain: 末段建议 try to recover with a short nap the next day rather than with more coffee，即第二天小睡补觉，故选 B。

items.title: Reading Section C 仔细阅读 2
items.paperTitle: 大学英语四级标准模拟卷 08
items.passage:
Every January, gyms fill with new members, and by March many of them have quietly disappeared. The pattern is so familiar that fitness staff call it the resolution curve. But a small group of researchers who study habit formation believe the problem is not motivation. It is the way people design their plans.

In one study, participants were asked to exercise three times a week for twelve weeks. Half of them were told to choose any time and place that suited them; the other half were asked to link the exercise to an existing daily routine, such as walking straight to the gym after a morning lecture. The second group attended about twice as many sessions. The explanation is simple: a new behaviour needs a reliable signal, and an existing routine provides one.

The researchers also found that starting very small helped. People who began with ten minutes on a bicycle were more likely to still be exercising after a month than those who began with an hour. Ten minutes feels too easy to skip, and once the habit exists it can be lengthened. A failed attempt at an ambitious plan, by contrast, often ends all attempts.

Social surroundings matter as well. Students who exercised with a friend attended more regularly, and those who told their roommates about their plan were less likely to give up. None of this requires money or special equipment. It requires a fixed moment, a small first step and someone who notices whether you turn up. That is probably why the oldest advice remains the best: put your sports shoes where you will see them in the morning.

questions.q: What is the resolution curve?
options: A kind of gym equipment.
A twelve-week training programme.
A method of measuring fitness.
The pattern of new members dropping out.
questions.explain: Passage 2 开头说健身房一月人满为患，三月许多人悄然消失，staff call it the resolution curve，即新会员退出的规律，故选 D。

questions.q: What made the second group in the study more successful?
options: They had more free time.
They linked exercise to an existing routine.
They exercised alone.
They chose expensive gyms.
questions.explain: 第二组被要求把锻炼与既有日常安排联系起来，如早上听完课直接去健身房，出勤次数约为第一组的两倍，故选 B。

questions.q: What does the passage say about starting small?
options: It makes people more likely to keep exercising.
It wastes the first month.
It is suitable only for children.
It requires a personal trainer.
questions.explain: 研究发现从每天十分钟开始的人一个月后仍在锻炼的比例更高，因为十分钟很容易做到，不会让人想跳过，故选 A。

items.title: Reading Section C 仔细阅读 1
items.paperTitle: 大学英语四级标准模拟卷 09
items.passage:
For most of the last century, city planners measured success by how quickly cars could move. Wider roads, longer crossings and more parking spaces were seen as progress. In the past two decades, however, a different measure has become popular: how many people walk.

The change began with public health. Doctors pointed out that sitting in a car for an hour a day contributes to obesity and heart disease, while walking for thirty minutes brings clear benefits. Cities that made walking easier soon noticed something else: shops on busy pedestrian streets sold more, because walkers stop and look, while drivers pass by. Property values along attractive walking routes rose as well.

Safety is the other half of the argument. In countries that redesigned streets to slow traffic, the number of serious accidents fell sharply. The most effective measures were simple and cheap: narrower lanes, raised crossings, more street trees and lower speed limits in residential areas. None of them required a new underground railway or a decade of construction.

There are limits. Pedestrian-friendly schemes can raise rents and push out the small businesses they were meant to help. People who live far from the centre may have no choice but to drive. And in very hot or very cold climates, walking is pleasant for only part of the year.

Even so, the direction of travel has changed. City governments increasingly publish plans in which the first question is not how to move cars faster, but how to make the first ten minutes of a journey on foot something people are willing to do.

questions.q: How did city planners measure success in the past?
options: By the number of pedestrians.
By the amount of green space.
By the speed of car traffic.
By the price of housing.
questions.explain: Passage 1 开头说 planners measured success by how quickly cars could move，即以汽车通行速度衡量成功，故选 C。

questions.q: Why did shops on pedestrian streets sell more?
options: Walkers stop and look at the windows.
Cars could park right outside.
Rents on those streets were lower.
The streets were much longer.
questions.explain: 第二段说 shops on busy pedestrian streets sold more, because walkers stop and look, while drivers pass by，即行人会停下观看，故选 A。

questions.q: Which measure is described as simple and cheap?
options: Building a new underground railway.
A decade of road construction.
Removing all the street trees.
Lower speed limits in residential areas.
questions.explain: 第三段列举的简单低成本措施包括 narrower lanes, raised crossings, more street trees and lower speed limits in residential areas，故选 D。

questions.q: What problem can pedestrian-friendly schemes cause?
options: More serious accidents.
Rising rents for local businesses.
Much colder winters.
Fewer shops in the city centre.
questions.explain: 第四段指出这类方案 can raise rents and push out the small businesses they were meant to help，即租金上涨可能挤走本要帮助的小商户，故选 B。

items.title: Reading Section C 仔细阅读 2
items.paperTitle: 大学英语四级标准模拟卷 09
items.passage:
When a city builds a new square, it usually publishes photographs of clean paving, new benches and young trees. What it cannot photograph is whether anyone will use the space. Planners have learned, often painfully, that an attractive public space may stay empty if people have no reason to be there.

The most successful public spaces share a few features. First, they are easy to reach on foot from busy streets, rather than hidden behind buildings. Second, they offer different kinds of activity at the same time: a playground for children, a quiet corner for older people, a cafe, a stretch of grass. A space used by only one group tends to feel unsafe to everybody else. Third, they allow people to stay without spending money, which is why benches matter so much.

Janet Byrne, who studies urban life, argues that the value of such places cannot be counted fully in economic terms. A good public space teaches a city how to behave, she says. Children meet adults who are not their parents; strangers learn to share a table; people who disagree about everything else still sit on the same bench. Her research in eight neighbourhoods found that residents who used a local square regularly were more likely to know their neighbours and to trust them.

That is not an argument for building a square everywhere. Some places need shops, housing or public transport more urgently. But when space is available, the cheapest improvements are often the most effective. A few benches, a working fountain and a rule that allows people to sit without buying anything can turn an empty area into the busiest part of a neighbourhood. Maintenance matters too: a broken fountain or a dirty bench quickly tells people that the space is not cared for.

questions.q: What do planners often fail to consider about a new square?
options: The cost of the paving.
The number of trees to plant.
Whether people will actually use it.
How it will look in photographs.
questions.explain: Passage 2 开头说照片拍不出的是 whether anyone will use the space，并指出漂亮的公共空间可能空无一人，故选 C。

questions.q: Why do successful public spaces offer several kinds of activity?
options: To earn more money from rent.
So that different groups feel welcome and safe.
To keep the space quiet and empty.
To save money on benches.
questions.explain: 第二段说只被某一群体使用的空间会让其他人感到不安全，多样活动能让儿童、老人等不同人群都愿意停留，故选 B。

questions.q: What does Janet Byrne say about the value of public spaces?
options: It can be fully measured in money.
It is mainly good for tourism.
It matters only for young children.
It teaches people how to live together.
questions.explain: Janet Byrne 说 A good public space teaches a city how to behave，并举例陌生人共用一张桌子、互相认识与信任，故选 D。

items.title: Reading Section C 仔细阅读 1
items.paperTitle: 大学英语四级标准模拟卷 10
items.passage:
Heading to a hotel in central Singapore, a guest may be greeted by a machine about a metre tall. It can check in guests, carry their luggage to the lift and answer simple questions in four languages. Robots like this one, once a rare sight, are becoming ordinary in hotels, hospitals, restaurants and shopping centres. According to industry data, the number of service robots sold worldwide has more than tripled in five years, and the pandemic accelerated the trend: businesses that had lost staff to illness or quarantine needed help fast.

Supporters point to clear advantages. Service robots work without breaks and handle repetitive tasks such as delivering medicine in hospitals or cleaning floors in shopping centres at night. In hospitals in Japan, robots carry meals and laundry, which saves nurses perhaps two hours a day, time that can be spent with patients. In some restaurants a small robot delivers dishes while the human staff talk to customers, which many managers say is a better use of their skills.

Yet the picture is not entirely bright. One survey of hotel guests found that although most people were curious about the robots, fewer than a third said they would trust one with a problem such as a lost booking. Others complained that asking a machine for advice felt cold and unhelpful. Cost is another barrier: a delivery robot may cost as much as a year's salary for a member of staff, and small businesses rarely have the money. Researchers in the field add a further warning. Robots work well when a task can be described step by step, and badly when the unexpected happens. A child running into the corridor or a confused elderly patient can stop a robot completely, and the solution usually arrives on two legs. The best results, these researchers say, come from teams in which robots do the carrying and people do the deciding.

questions.q: What does the passage say about the number of service robots sold worldwide?
options: It has doubled in ten years.
It has more than tripled in five years.
It fell sharply during the pandemic.
It has stayed the same for a decade.
questions.explain: Passage 1 首段说 the number of service robots sold worldwide has more than tripled in five years，即五年间增长了两倍多，故选 B；疫情期间是加快了趋势而非下降，C 错。

questions.q: What do robots do in Japanese hospitals, according to the passage?
options: They carry out operations on patients.
They talk to patients about their illness.
They carry meals and laundry, saving nurses about two hours a day.
They check the work of doctors.
questions.explain: 第二段说 In hospitals in Japan, robots carry meals and laundry, which saves nurses perhaps two hours a day，故选 C；文中并未说机器人做手术或与病人讨论病情。

questions.q: What did the survey of hotel guests find?
options: Fewer than a third would trust a robot with a problem such as a lost booking.
Most guests refused to enter a hotel with robots.
Guests preferred robots to human staff in every situation.
Guests were willing to pay more for robot service.
questions.explain: 第三段说虽然多数客人对机器人好奇，but fewer than a third said they would trust one with a problem such as a lost booking，故选 A。

questions.q: What do researchers say about the limits of service robots?
options: They are too expensive for hospitals to buy.
They make more mistakes than tired people do.
They need to be replaced every two years.
They work badly when the unexpected happens.
questions.explain: 末段说 Robots work well when a task can be described step by step, and badly when the unexpected happens，并举小孩跑进走廊为例，故选 D。

items.title: Reading Section C 仔细阅读 2
items.paperTitle: 大学英语四级标准模拟卷 10
items.passage:
For most of the twentieth century, the phrase learning a trade meant learning one skill well and using it for thirty years. Automation has made that model much less reliable. A machine can now handle the filing, the calculations and even some of the writing that once filled a working day, and the tasks it cannot yet handle change faster than any syllabus can be rewritten. The result is a quiet shift in what employers say they need.

A survey of two thousand companies in Asia and Europe found that the three abilities most often named in job advertisements were not technical at all. They were the ability to communicate clearly, to solve unfamiliar problems and to learn something new quickly. Technical skills still matter, the report says, but they are no longer a guarantee of security; they are the entry ticket. What keeps a person employed is the capacity to add a second, related skill: a driver who learns to service electric vehicles, a nurse who learns to manage health data, a warehouse worker who becomes a robot maintenance assistant.

Some governments have begun to design training around this idea. Instead of funding short courses in one occupation, they offer workers paid time to study for a certificate in a nearby field, and some companies have copied the scheme. The early results are encouraging but modest. In one programme, about sixty per cent of participants finished the course, and three quarters of those who finished were still in work a year later. The researchers who evaluated the programme noted one unexpected detail: workers who studied with a colleague were twice as likely to finish. The deeper lesson may be about schools rather than factories. Students who have learned how to learn, and who are not afraid of being beginners, adapt most easily. A curriculum that rewards the right answer above the honest question may be training people for a world that is already disappearing.

questions.q: What has made the old model of learning a trade unreliable?
options: Fewer young people want to work in factories.
Automation now does tasks that once filled a working day.
Companies have stopped offering training.
Trade schools have closed down.
questions.explain: Passage 2 首段说 Automation has made that model much less reliable，并说明机器已能处理归档、计算乃至部分写作，「曾占满工作日」的任务被机器接手，故选 B。

questions.q: Which abilities did the survey find most often named in job advertisements?
options: Programming and bookkeeping.
Driving and operating machines.
Clear communication, problem solving and quick learning.
Foreign languages and public speaking.
questions.explain: 第二段列出招聘广告中最常提到的三项能力：communicate clearly, solve unfamiliar problems, learn something new quickly，故选 C。

questions.q: What unexpected detail did the researchers note about the training programme?
options: Older workers finished faster than young ones.
The courses were too expensive to continue.
Most participants left their jobs afterwards.
Workers who studied with a colleague were twice as likely to finish.
questions.explain: 第三段说 the researchers noted one unexpected detail: workers who studied with a colleague were twice as likely to finish，故选 D。

items.title: Reading Section C 仔细阅读 1
items.paperTitle: 2023年12月大学英语四级真题风格卷（原创题面）
items.passage:
Not long ago, an audiobook meant a set of CDs borrowed from a library. Today it is the fastest-growing part of the publishing industry: sales have risen by double digits every year for a decade, and in some markets one book in five is now read through headphones. The reasons are practical. A commute, a gym session or a pile of washing-up becomes reading time, and listeners who had stopped buying paper books often become readers again.

Publishers responded quickly, hiring actors and paying for studios and sound effects. Some well-known titles now have two versions, one in a single familiar voice and one with a full cast, and a few authors have begun to write with narration in mind, shortening long descriptions that sound slow when spoken. For language learners the format has an obvious attraction: the written text and its careful pronunciation are never far apart.

Not everyone is delighted. Teachers who study reading worry that listening is a different skill. A reader who skips back to check a sentence is doing something a listener rarely does, and the attention demanded by a complicated argument may be lost when the voice continues without pause. A study of university students found that those who only listened remembered fewer details of a chapter than those who read it on paper, although they remembered the main idea equally well.

The most sensible view may be that the two forms do different jobs. Stories and interviews suit the ear, while a textbook or a contract still asks for the eye. What is striking, however, is that the argument itself has changed. A decade ago people asked whether listening counted as reading. Now they ask when it is the better choice.

questions.q: What is said about audiobook sales?
options: They have grown by double digits every year for a decade.
They fell as soon as streaming services appeared.
They are now larger than printed book sales.
They depend mainly on university libraries.
questions.explain: Passage 1 首段说 sales have risen by double digits every year for a decade，即连续十年保持两位数增长，故选 A；文中只说在某些市场每五本书有一本以有声形式阅读，并未说销量超过纸质书，C 过度推断。

questions.q: Why have some authors begun to write with narration in mind?
options: They are paid more for audio editions.
They no longer write for libraries.
They want their books to be made into films.
They want their books to sound good when read aloud.
questions.explain: 第二段说有些作者开始 with narration in mind, shortening long descriptions that sound slow when spoken，即为了让文字朗读出来效果好，故选 D。

questions.q: What did the study of university students find?
options: Listeners understood the main idea worse than readers.
Listeners remembered the main idea but fewer details.
Students preferred audio to paper in every subject.
Most students gave up halfway through the chapter.
questions.explain: 第三段说 those who only listened remembered fewer details of a chapter than those who read it on paper, although they remembered the main idea equally well，故选 B。

questions.q: What is the author's conclusion about the two forms of reading?
options: They suit different kinds of books.
Paper books will disappear within a decade.
Listening should replace reading in schools.
Audio editions are cheaper to produce.
questions.explain: 末段说 the two forms do different jobs，故事与访谈适合听，教科书与合同仍需用眼，即两种形式适合不同种类的书，故选 A。

items.title: Reading Section C 仔细阅读 2
items.paperTitle: 2023年12月大学英语四级真题风格卷（原创题面）
items.passage:
The Rex was the only cinema in a town of nine thousand people, and when it closed in 2011 the building was sold and used for storing animal feed. For four years the town had nothing but the television in the pub. Then a retired teacher, Mary Appleton, asked at a public meeting whether people would pay five pounds a month to own a cinema. To her surprise, three hundred households said yes on the spot.

The Rex reopened two years later as a community cinema. It is run by a committee of twelve volunteers: a former electrician looks after the projector, two teenagers run the ticket desk on Saturdays, and Mary, now seventy-eight, chooses most of the films. The programme mixes new releases with old favourites, and once a month a local historian introduces a film connected with the area. Tickets are cheaper than in the city, and a small grant pays for free screenings for school classes.

Running a cinema is not easy. The projector broke down twice last year, and the committee spent a month deciding whether to spend nearly all its savings on a digital system. Membership has slipped slightly as streaming services have grown. Yet the audiences keep coming, and not always for the film. On a Friday night in winter, the Rex is one of the few warm, noisy places in town where people of different ages sit in the same room. Mary says that is the point. The films matter, she explains, but what people are really buying is an evening out with their neighbours.

questions.q: What happened to the cinema building after the cinema closed in 2011?
options: It was turned into a pub.
It stood empty for ten years.
It was used for storing animal feed.
It became a school hall.
questions.explain: Passage 2 首段说 the building was sold and used for storing animal feed，故选 C；文中说此后四年小镇只有酒馆里的电视，并未说电影院变成了酒馆，A 为张冠李戴。

questions.q: How is the Rex run now?
options: By a national cinema chain.
By a committee of twelve volunteers.
By the local government alone.
By the retired teacher on her own.
questions.explain: 第二段说 It is run by a committee of twelve volunteers，故选 B；Mary 只是其中负责选片的一员，并非独自经营，D 不准确。

questions.q: What difficulty is mentioned in the passage?
options: Few films are available for the small screen.
Young people are unwilling to work there.
The town has decided to close the cinema again.
Membership has slipped as streaming services have grown.
questions.explain: 第三段说 Membership has slipped slightly as streaming services have grown，即流媒体兴起使会员人数略有下降，故选 D。

items.title: Reading Section C 仔细阅读 1
items.paperTitle: 2024年6月大学英语四级真题风格卷（原创题面）
items.passage:
Each autumn, thousands of students arrive at university straight from school, and a small but growing number arrive a year later, after a gap year. The idea of taking a year off between school and university used to worry parents, who imagined a year of sleeping late and playing computer games. Research suggests a different picture. In Britain, where the practice has been studied for decades, students who took a structured gap year, working, volunteering or travelling with a purpose, are slightly less likely to drop out and slightly more likely to finish with a good degree. The effect is small, and researchers are careful not to overstate it. Students who take a gap year are already, on average, more confident and better organized than those who do not, so it is hard to separate the year from the person.

What the evidence does support is narrower. A year of doing something difficult, teaching in a rural school, working in a restaurant kitchen or learning a language badly before learning it better, gives young people a kind of confidence that classrooms rarely produce. They discover that they can be useful, that adults will listen to them, and that failure is survivable. They also learn what they do not want to do, which can be as valuable as discovering a career.

For families considering it, the practical advice from universities is simple. The year should have a plan, a purpose and someone to report back to; it does not need to be expensive or far away. A gap year spent well is not a year off. It is a year of a completely different kind of learning.

questions.q: What does the British research suggest about a structured gap year?
options: It is useful only for students who failed their school exams.
It is linked to slightly better results at university.
It makes students much more likely to drop out.
It costs more than a year of university study.
questions.explain: Passage 1 首段说学生 slightly less likely to drop out and slightly more likely to finish with a good degree，即与更好的学业结果略有相关，故选 B。

questions.q: Why is it hard to separate the effect of the gap year from the person?
options: Gap-year students rarely answer surveys.
Universities keep no records of gap years.
Gap-year activities are too different to compare.
Students who take a gap year are already more confident and organized.
questions.explain: 首段末尾说 Students who take a gap year are already, on average, more confident and better organized than those who do not, so it is hard to separate the year from the person，故选 D。

questions.q: What do young people gain from doing something difficult for a year?
options: A guaranteed place on a prestigious course.
Higher marks in their final school exams.
Confidence and the knowledge that failure is survivable.
A career plan chosen by their parents.
questions.explain: 第二段说他们发现自己有用、大人会听他们说话，and that failure is survivable，即获得自信并明白失败可以承受，故选 C。

questions.q: What practical advice does the passage give to families?
options: The year should have a plan, a purpose and someone to report back to.
The year should be spent as far from home as possible.
The year must be paid for by the university.
The year should be kept secret from friends.
questions.explain: 末段建议 The year should have a plan, a purpose and someone to report back to，并说不必昂贵或远行，故选 A。

items.title: Reading Section C 仔细阅读 2
items.paperTitle: 2024年6月大学英语四级真题风格卷（原创题面）
items.passage:
Ten years ago most shop owners on a British high street would have described the internet as a problem. Online shops were cheaper, took no rent and never closed, and one in eight high-street shops stood empty. The survivors have gradually discovered a different way to use the internet: not to sell, but to be found.

The most successful examples are surprisingly simple. A hardware shop in Sheffield became known across the country after the owner began filming two-minute videos of unusual repairs, such as mending an old lamp or a broken pram. The videos cost nothing and took a few minutes to make, but customers now travel from three neighbouring towns, and the shop sells more of the parts it once kept for years on the shelf. A bakery in a small town posts a photograph of the morning's bread each day at six, and its queue of regulars has grown. What these shops have in common is not a large budget but a habit: someone posts two or three times a week, in a voice that sounds like a person rather than a leaflet.

The change is not free. It takes an hour or two of an owner's evening, and owners who post for a month and then stop often report no benefit at all. Misleading reviews are another trouble; one shop now answers every review, good or bad, because the reply is read by the next hundred customers. Yet the shopkeepers interviewed for a recent report were almost all optimistic. As one of them put it, the internet cannot deliver a pair of boots to your door, but it can remind you which door to knock on.

questions.q: What was the situation of the typical British high street ten years ago?
options: Online shopping had not yet appeared.
Rents on the high street were falling fast.
One in eight shops stood empty.
Shop owners were already filming videos.
questions.explain: Passage 2 首段说 online shops were cheaper, took no rent and never closed, and one in eight high-street shops stood empty，故选 C。

questions.q: What made the hardware shop in Sheffield well known?
options: Its very low prices.
Short videos of unusual repairs.
A television advertisement.
A large online delivery service.
questions.explain: 第二段说 the owner began filming two-minute videos of unusual repairs，随后全国知名，故选 B。

questions.q: What do the successful shops have in common?
options: They all employ a marketing agency.
They sell only products made locally.
They open seven days a week.
They post regularly in a voice that sounds personal.
questions.explain: 第二段末尾说它们的共同点不是大预算而是习惯：someone posts two or three times a week, in a voice that sounds like a person，故选 D。

items.title: Reading Section C 仔细阅读 1
items.paperTitle: 2024年12月大学英语四级真题风格卷（原创题面）
items.passage:
Smartwatches are no longer just a way to check messages. Millions of people now use them to count their steps, measure their heart rate and track how well they sleep. Health authorities have welcomed the trend: when people can see their own data, the argument goes, they are more likely to take exercise and less likely to ignore warning signs.

Yet doctors are increasingly cautious about the numbers. A wrist device is not a medical instrument. Its heart rate readings can be disturbed by movement, its sleep measurement is based on guesswork, and its step count depends on how the device is worn. One study found that two popular models differed by nearly 15 percent when counting the same walk. More troubling is the effect on anxious users. Some check their heart rate dozens of times a day and are convinced that a minor change means serious illness, so they visit clinics that are already busy. Some doctors now ask such patients to bring a month of readings rather than a single number, which gives a fairer picture and saves time in the consultation.

None of this means that wearable devices are useless. They are good at showing long-term patterns. A slow fall in daily activity over several weeks can be a helpful signal for a doctor, and a simple reminder to stand up every hour may do more good than an expensive health plan. What matters is how the data is used. As one cardiologist put it, a watch can tell you that something has changed. It cannot tell you why, and it certainly cannot replace a conversation with a doctor.

questions.q: Why have health authorities welcomed the use of smartwatches?
options: They believe visible data encourages healthier habits.
They want to collect personal data for hospitals.
They think watches can replace family doctors.
They hope to sell more devices to young people.
questions.explain: 第一段说卫生部门欢迎这一趋势，理由是当人们能看到自己的数据时更可能锻炼、更少忽视警示信号，故选 A。

questions.q: What does the author say about the accuracy of wrist devices?
options: It is better than that of hospital equipment.
It can be affected by movements and other factors.
It has improved greatly in recent months.
It is accurate enough for medical diagnosis.
questions.explain: 第二段说腕表的心率读数会受运动干扰，睡眠数据靠推测，计步取决于佩戴方式，两款机型计步相差近 15%，故选 B。

questions.q: What problem do anxious users cause?
options: They stop taking any exercise.
They damage their watches quickly.
They buy more devices than they need.
They add pressure on busy clinics.
questions.explain: 第二段末说焦虑用户一天查看心率几十次，稍有变化就以为得了重病，于是去本就繁忙的诊所就诊，故选 D。

questions.q: What is the author's view of wearable devices?
options: They should be banned in hospitals.
They are a waste of money for most people.
They are useful for spotting long-term patterns.
They will soon replace regular health checks.
questions.explain: 第三段说可穿戴设备并非无用，它们善于显示长期趋势，例如数周内活动量缓慢下降可以是给医生的有用信号，故选 C。

items.title: Reading Section C 仔细阅读 2
items.paperTitle: 2024年12月大学英语四级真题风格卷（原创题面）
items.passage:
Twenty years ago, bottled water seemed to be the future. Supermarkets devoted whole aisles to it, restaurants proudly poured it, and carrying a plastic bottle became a habit for commuters and students alike. Today the picture looks different. Across Europe and parts of Asia, cities are installing public refill stations and handing out reusable bottles, and a growing number of shops and cafes allow customers to fill up for free.

The argument for refill stations is partly about waste. A single plastic bottle may take hundreds of years to break down, and even when it is recycled, the process uses energy and water. Refill stations, by contrast, serve thousands of people from one pipe. Supporters also point to cost: tap water is far cheaper than the bottled kind, and they question whether the difference in taste is as great as advertising suggests. In blind tests, many volunteers cannot tell one from the other, and restaurants and offices have begun to install refill points of their own.

But the movement has its critics. Some consumers worry about the quality of tap water, especially in cities where the pipes are old.
