paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Every year thousands of books are left in the green boxes outside the charity's office. Some come from families whose children have grown up; others are sent by schools replacing their library stock, and a few publishers donate damaged but readable copies. A small van collects the boxes twice a week and takes them to a warehouse on the edge of the city. Last year alone the charity received more than ninety thousand books, which is both a wonderful problem and a serious one, because every single copy has to be handled.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Inside the warehouse, volunteers work in teams of six. One group checks each book for missing pages, water damage and writing on the pages, and anything beyond repair goes to a recycling centre. Another group sorts the rest into categories: picture books, novels, science, history and reference. A third group stamps the charity's name inside the cover. On a busy Saturday the teams can process about four thousand books, which sounds impressive until you remember how many are waiting.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Before a box is sent anywhere, staff contact the school that will receive it. They ask the head teacher how many students there are, what ages they teach and which subjects need materials. A school with no laboratory may ask for science books, while one in a rural area may simply want stories to encourage reading in English. Sending the wrong books wastes money and disappoints children, so the charity keeps a list of requests and matches each donation to a school.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Getting the boxes to the schools is the hardest part. Lorries can reach towns on main roads, but many schools lie at the end of dirt tracks that become mud in the rainy season. In those places the boxes are transferred to motorbikes, which carry two at a time up the hills. Drivers sometimes wait for days for the weather to improve. The charity now stores books in regional depots so that the final journey is short, even if the first one is long.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Books alone do not create readers. Before a delivery, two trainers spend a week with the teachers, showing them how to run a reading club, how to read aloud with expression and how to let children choose books for themselves. The teachers are also given simple record cards so that they can see which pupils are reading and which are not. Most schools ask for the training again the following year, and some have started their own libraries with the skills they learned.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The results are easiest to see in the children's faces. In one mountain school, a girl of ten told a volunteer that she had never owned a book before and asked whether she could keep it. Teachers report that pupils who join the reading club attend school more regularly and write longer stories. Numbers cannot measure everything, but the charity's own survey found that reading confidence had risen sharply in almost every school it visited.

statements.text: Donated books are examined and sorted into groups before they are sent out.
Some books have to be carried by motorbike where lorries cannot reach.
The charity asks each school which titles and subjects its students actually need.
Books come from families, schools and publishers rather than being bought new.
Teachers are given training so that they can use the books in their lessons.

items.title: Reading Section B 长篇阅读匹配
items.paperTitle: 大学英语四级标准模拟卷 02

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Banks, bus companies and government offices have moved most of their services onto the internet, and the change has left many older people behind. A person who once paid every bill at the counter may now be asked to download an app, create a password and confirm a code sent by message. For those who have never owned a smartphone, these small tasks can feel like a locked door. The charity behind the sessions says that calls for help have doubled in three years, and most come from people over seventy.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The sessions take place on Tuesday and Friday mornings in a quiet room at the back of the town library. Volunteers put out long tables, a kettle and a box of written instructions in large print. Learners arrive with their own phones, often still in the box, and sit beside the volunteer they have been paired with. There is no lecture and no fixed programme; people bring the problems they met during the week, and the room slowly fills with quiet conversation.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The first lesson is always the same. Learners practise switching the phone on and off, making a call, sending a short message and adding a name to the contacts list. Only when these actions feel natural do they move on to photographs or the internet. Volunteers say it is a mistake to begin with the most exciting features; a person who cannot answer a call will soon lose confidence. Simple actions are repeated until they become habits, and each small success makes the next lesson easier.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Each learner works with the same student volunteer every week. This pairing matters more than it might seem. The volunteer learns what the person already knows, which buttons frighten them and how quickly they tire, and the learner does not have to explain the same difficulties to a stranger each time. One volunteer describes her role as a patient neighbour rather than a teacher. When her learner finally sent a photograph to her grandchild, she says, both of them were close to tears.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Not every danger comes from a broken phone. Volunteers spend a full session on fraud, because older people are often targeted by callers pretending to be from a bank. Learners are shown how to recognise a suspicious message, why they should never share a password or bank details, and what to do if money has already been taken. The advice is written on a card that fits in a purse. Several learners have since stopped a scam themselves, and one brought the card to the police station to show an officer.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The charity measures success in small events: a first video call with a grandchild, a bus ticket bought on the phone, a photograph sent to a friend. These moments rarely appear in national statistics, but they change a person's week. Volunteers also report a benefit they did not expect. Many learners stay after the session for tea and begin to help each other, so the room has become a social club as much as a classroom. The project now runs in eleven towns, and the waiting list grows every month.

statements.text: New learners first practise simple actions such as switching the phone on and making a call.
Learners are warned not to give bank details to strangers who call or send messages.
More and more older people need help as everyday services move online.
Each learner is paired with one student who can go at the learner's own speed.
Volunteers hold regular sessions in a quiet room of the local library.

items.title: Reading Section B 长篇阅读匹配
items.paperTitle: 大学英语四级标准模拟卷 03

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: A green roof is exactly what its name suggests: a building whose flat top has been covered with soil and plants. Under the visible layer there are several others that most people never see — a waterproof membrane, a drainage system and a root barrier. The weight has to be calculated before anything is planted, and older buildings sometimes need extra support. Once the layers are in place, the roof can be planted with grass, moss, wild flowers or small shrubs, depending on how much weight the structure can carry.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Cities are usually several degrees warmer than the countryside around them, because concrete and asphalt absorb heat during the day and release it slowly at night. Plants work in the opposite way. They take up water and release it as vapour, a process that cools the air, and the soil beneath them insulates the building, so less energy is needed for air conditioning. Measurements on a green roof in summer have found the surface temperature to be up to thirty degrees lower than that of a conventional roof next door.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: When a heavy storm arrives, drains in a modern city can be overwhelmed within minutes. A green roof slows the water down. Rain is caught by the plants and soil, and what does not evaporate or is taken up by the roots runs off more slowly, sometimes hours after the rain has stopped. In cities that have suffered from flooding, this delay is valuable. Green roofs cannot replace proper drainage, engineers warn, but they can reduce the peak load on a system during the worst hour of a storm.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A city centre is a difficult place for a bird, a bee or a butterfly. Green roofs create small islands of habitat above the traffic, and research in several European cities has recorded bees, beetles and nesting birds on them. The value depends on the plants chosen: a roof covered with a single type of moss supports far less life than one planted with a mixture of flowers and grasses. Connecting such roofs across a district, rather than building one isolated example, makes a real difference to insects that need stepping stones between green spaces.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The obvious objection is cost. Installing a green roof can cost two or three times as much as a standard one, and the building owner may not stay long enough to see the savings. Supporters reply that the calculation is wider than the roof itself. The roof lasts longer because the membrane is protected from sunlight, the building uses less energy for cooling, and the city saves money on drainage. Some cities now offer grants or allow developers to build higher when they include a green roof, which changes the sums for everyone involved.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Green roofs are no longer an experiment. In Singapore, new buildings are required to include planting on their roofs, and the city's most famous hotel has a garden that runs along its top like a park. In Germany, the idea has been common for decades, and several cities offer financial support. Closer to home, schools and offices have used their flat roofs for gardens, vegetable plots and even small sports areas. Supporters say the examples are spreading because the benefits are easy to explain, and a visitor can see them from street level.

statements.text: A green roof can slow the flow of rainwater into drains during heavy storms.
These roofs offer food and shelter to birds and insects in crowded cities.
A green roof is a layer of plants and soil placed on top of a building.
The idea is now required by law in some cities and supported with money in others.
Plants reduce the heat that buildings absorb and release into the streets.

items.title: Reading Section B 长篇阅读匹配
items.paperTitle: 大学英语四级标准模拟卷 04

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For most of the twentieth century a museum was a quiet hall of glass cases, and the visitor's job was to look. Curators now describe their work differently: they want people to leave with a story rather than a list of dates. Labels have grown longer, and rooms are arranged around questions instead of centuries. In one city museum, the first object a visitor meets is not a crown but a schoolboy's letter written in 1916.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Families were once tolerated rather than welcomed. Today many museums run special mornings when the lights are brighter, the paths are shorter and touching is allowed. Staff are trained to kneel down when they speak to a six-year-old. The change is not only generous; it is practical. Children who enjoy a visit bring their parents back, and school groups have become one of the most reliable sources of income for smaller museums.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Museums are also opening their back doors. Several now rent desk space to researchers, run evening language classes and allow students to use their libraries after dark. A museum in Manchester offers a quiet study room to local teenagers during the exam season. Its director argues that a building which belongs to the public should be useful every day, not only on the two afternoons a week when most tourists appear.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: None of this is easy to pay for. Government grants have fallen in many countries, and the cost of heating an old stone building keeps rising. Some museums have introduced ticket prices, a decision that always causes argument. Others lend objects to commercial exhibitions abroad. Most directors agree that a museum cannot survive on charm alone, and that a clear financial plan matters as much as a good exhibition.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: In the past, decisions were made by experts behind closed doors. Some museums now invite residents to choose what should be displayed. In one town, a public meeting decided that the museum's largest room should be given to the history of local factories rather than to a collection of coins. Attendance doubled within a year. Visitors say they come because the place finally speaks about their own streets and families.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The danger of chasing visitors is that a museum may lose the very thing that makes it valuable. If every room must be interactive and every label amusing, objects become background. Critics point out that serious research and slow-looking exhibitions are expensive and rarely attract headlines. The best institutions, they argue, keep a balance: a noisy family morning on Saturday does not mean that Tuesday afternoon has to be full of screens.

statements.text: Some museums hold special mornings so that young children may touch objects and walk shorter distances.
Curators now hope visitors will remember a story instead of a series of facts.
Some museums let students use their libraries and offer quiet rooms during exam seasons.
Falling public funding and rising heating costs have led some museums to charge for entry.
In one town, residents chose to give the largest room to the history of local industry.

items.title: Reading Section B 长篇阅读匹配
items.paperTitle: 大学英语四级标准模拟卷 05

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: The story began with a piece of land behind a bus stop, covered in weeds and broken bottles. In 2016 a group of residents asked the city council whether they could grow vegetables there. The answer was a one-year trial. They cleared the ground with borrowed tools, built twelve raised beds and carried the soil in wheelbarrows. Nothing about the site was beautiful, yet by the end of the first summer strangers were stopping to look over the fence and to ask whether they could join the waiting list.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: A garden with forty members needs a system. Each household looks after one bed and one shared job: the compost, the water pipes, the tools or the notice board. Two people open the gate on weekday mornings, and a rota covers the weekends. Nobody is paid, and nobody is allowed to do everything. Members say the rota matters more than the rules on paper, because it shows new members how much work one tomato plant demands.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Nearby primary schools treat the garden as an open-air classroom. Classes come in spring and autumn to plant beans, measure growth and draw what they see. One teacher uses the garden to teach science, another to discuss healthy eating. Children who refuse vegetables at school lunch often eat them raw here. For many of them this is the first time they have seen food growing in soil rather than arriving in a plastic bag on a supermarket shelf.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Harvest day falls on the last Saturday of the month. Members keep what they need, and the rest goes to a small table by the gate with a sign saying 'help yourself'. Some of it reaches elderly neighbours who can no longer shop easily, and some goes to a food bank two streets away. The gardeners do not regard this as charity; they simply believe that a place which grows food should also feed the street around it.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: No garden is peaceful all the time. Arguments have been about water bills, about loud music and about a plum tree that shaded someone's tomatoes. The committee's answer is to meet for twenty minutes on harvest day, with a rule that nobody may discuss a problem at the gate. Most disagreements are settled there; when one is not, the member who feels unheard may bring it to the council officer who supervises the site.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The one-year trial ended long ago, but the land remains uncertain. The council could sell the site for housing, and the gardeners know that a good season proves nothing about the lease. In 2022 they helped to write a neighbourhood plan which keeps the garden in public use for fifteen years. Meanwhile they plant fruit trees, which will take years to fruit. 'You do not plant a tree for yourself,' one member says. 'You plant it for whoever comes next.'

statements.text: The garden started when residents turned an empty piece of land into something productive.
Members take turns to look after shared jobs, and the rota teaches newcomers how much work is involved.
School classes visit the garden so that pupils can see how vegetables are grown.
Part of the produce is given to older neighbours and to a food bank.
It is still not certain that the garden can stay on the land in the long term.

items.title: Reading Section B 长篇阅读匹配
items.paperTitle: 大学英语四级标准模拟卷 06

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: It started with two neighbours and a borrowed table. In 2015, a retired teacher and a restaurant owner in the Riverside district decided that the many foreign families in their street should have a chance to meet the older residents. They set up one table outside the community centre with dumplings on one side and bread on the other. About thirty people came. The following year the district office offered a small square, and the festival was born.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Food remains the centre of the event. Last year forty cooking stalls stretched along the river, and the queue for a Vietnamese soup was longer than the queue for anything else. Cooks are encouraged to stand beside their dishes and explain what is in them, so that visitors leave with a recipe rather than only a memory. Every stall must offer at least one small portion for a token price, so that a family with children can try many things.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The stage is deliberately mixed. A professional folk group from the local theatre performs in the afternoon, but the evening programme belongs to amateurs: a primary school choir, a group of students learning flamenco, and a band of neighbours who met at the festival two years ago. Auditions are open to anyone, and the only rule is that each act must last no more than eight minutes, since a tired audience stops listening and starts queuing for food.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Behind the scenes, about sixty volunteers keep the festival running. They guide visitors who cannot find a stall, hand out programmes at the bridge, help elderly residents find seats and collect rubbish at the end of the night. New volunteers attend a short briefing a week in advance, and each is paired with someone who worked the previous year. Organisers say the volunteers, not the stage, decide whether the festival feels friendly.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Money is the permanent worry. The district provides the square and pays for electricity, but everything else must be found. Two years ago a sudden storm destroyed half the tents, and the festival ended with a debt. Since then the organisers have asked local businesses for support, in exchange for a line on the programme. A cloth bag with the festival logo also raises a modest but reliable sum each year.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Success has brought a new problem: size. Some residents now complain about noise, traffic and litter, and the district has asked the organisers to keep the event inside the square. Others would like to see it grow into a three-day fair that attracts visitors from other cities. The committee has postponed any decision for a year and, in the meantime, has begun to count how many people arrive by bicycle.

statements.text: Cooks stand beside their dishes and explain the ingredients, so visitors can take recipes home.
The festival began when two neighbours decided to bring foreign families and older residents together.
The evening programme is given to ordinary residents, including a school choir and a student group.
New helpers receive a short introduction and work alongside someone with experience.
After a storm left the event in debt, the organisers turned to local businesses for support.

items.title: Reading Section B 长篇阅读匹配
items.paperTitle: 大学英语四级标准模拟卷 07

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Growing demand Farmers' markets were once a small weekend activity in a few towns. Over the past decade their number has grown steadily, and many now run twice a week. Part of the reason is that shoppers ask more questions about food: where it was grown, when it was picked and how it was transported. Stallholders can answer these questions directly, which supermarkets, with their long supply chains, find much harder to do.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: A shorter journey Food sold at a market usually travels only a few miles from field to stall. That means it can be picked closer to ripeness, and it does not need the cold storage that long-distance transport requires. Several studies suggest that local produce can also lose fewer nutrients. The saving in transport is real, though researchers caution that small deliveries made by many individual vans may not always be greener overall.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Bringing people together A market is more than a place to buy vegetables. Regular customers learn the names of stallholders, and neighbours meet while queuing for bread. In some towns the market has become the centre of community life, hosting cooking demonstrations and children's activities. Shopkeepers nearby report that the visitors also spend money in their businesses, so the benefit spreads beyond the stalls themselves.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Challenges for small farmers Running a stall is hard work. Farmers must leave home before dawn, pay for the pitch and still look after their land. Bad weather can ruin a whole day's income. Some smaller producers have joined together to share a stall and transport costs. Without such cooperation, many would find that selling directly takes more time than they can spare from actual farming.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Changing habits of young people Market organisers say the average customer is getting younger. Students and young professionals come for a cheap lunch, then leave with unfamiliar vegetables they have never cooked before. Online videos have helped: a short clip showing how to prepare a strange-looking root can turn it into a bestseller the following weekend. This experimentation is slowly changing the way young people plan their meals.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: What the future may hold Most people involved in farmers' markets are optimistic. As food prices rise and concern about the environment grows, buying directly from producers looks attractive. Permanent indoor market halls, card payments and home delivery are already appearing in some cities. Observers warn, however, that rising rents may push markets away from the very neighbourhoods that need them most.

statements.text: Shoppers increasingly want to know where their food comes from and how it was produced.
Markets give local residents a place to meet and talk, not just to shop.
Younger customers are trying unfamiliar vegetables and changing how they plan meals.
Selling locally means the food is fresher and needs less transport and storage.
Organisers believe markets will keep growing as people seek sustainable food.

items.title: Reading Section B 长篇阅读匹配
items.paperTitle: 大学英语四级标准模拟卷 08

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Time away from screens Parents who are tired of arguing about screen time have found a simple alternative: a box of cards or a board. A recent survey of 2,000 families found that four in ten now play games together at least once a week, and most of them say the main reason is to spend an evening without phones. Teachers report similar experiments in classrooms, where short games are used to warm up a lesson.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Old games, new players Games that grandparents played are returning to the shelves. Shops report strong demand for new editions of classic word and card games, often bought by people in their twenties and thirties. Designers have improved the artwork and shortened the rules, so a game that once took an hour to explain can now be taught in five minutes. Social media has helped, as players share photographs of their evenings online.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A boost for small shops In many cities, board game cafes have opened in the past few years. Customers pay a small fee, borrow games from the shelves and order drinks while they play. For the owners of small shops, this is a way to compete with online retailers: what is being sold is not the box but an evening out. Some cafes also run tournaments that fill quiet weekday evenings.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Learning to lose Teachers and psychologists point to benefits that have little to do with the games themselves. Waiting for your turn, explaining a plan, disagreeing without losing your temper and accepting defeat are all practised at the table. One primary school now holds a weekly game afternoon and says arguments in the playground have become less frequent, because pupils have learned to separate the result of a game from the person who won it.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Barriers to growth Not everything is easy. Translating and printing a game for a new market can cost far more than the designers expect, and small publishers struggle to compete with large companies. Illegal copies appear quickly online. Designers also complain that a successful idea is imitated within months, and that the law offers little protection to a set of rules or a piece of cardboard.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The table as a meeting place For adults who move to a new city, a games evening can be an unusually easy way to meet people. Unlike a party, it gives strangers something to do and a reason to talk. Organisers of public game nights say that regulars often arrive alone and leave in groups, and that the atmosphere is friendlier than in a bar, because everyone is concentrating on the same table.

statements.text: Independent shops and cafes have appeared where customers pay to play games together.
Many families choose games as a way to spend an evening without screens.
Playing games teaches children to accept defeat and wait their turn.
Game nights give newcomers and neighbours a chance to meet and make friends.
Classic games are attracting interest from a younger generation.

items.title: Reading Section B 长篇阅读匹配
items.paperTitle: 大学英语四级标准模拟卷 09

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Slower journeys, richer experiences A journey that takes ten hours is usually seen as a problem. Supporters of slow travel see it differently: the hours are part of the holiday. From a train window you notice villages, rivers and fields that disappear when you fly. You can also stop halfway, spend a night in a town you had never heard of, and continue the next morning. Many travellers say the unplanned stops are what they remember longest.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Night trains return to the timetable After years of decline, overnight trains are appearing again on European timetables. New routes link cities such as Vienna, Paris and Stockholm, and several more are planned. The appeal is obvious: you sleep while you move, and you arrive in the centre of a city rather than at an airport far from it. Tickets are not always cheap, however, and popular cabins sell out months in advance.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The cost of going slowly Slow travel has a price. A train ticket booked late can cost more than a budget flight, and every extra night in a hotel adds to the total. People with limited holidays may also find that two days of travelling leaves less time for the destination. For families, the cheaper option is often still the car, especially when luggage and children are taken into account. The choice, travellers admit, is rarely simple.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A smaller footprint Transport is a major source of greenhouse gases, and aviation is one of the fastest-growing parts of it. Measured per passenger, a train journey within Europe typically produces a small fraction of the carbon dioxide of the same trip by plane. This is the strongest argument for slow travel, and it is the one that governments mention most often when they promote rail. Yet the total number of flights continues to rise.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Business travellers stay away For all the enthusiasm, slow travel remains a leisure activity. Companies rarely pay for an employee to spend two days on a train when a flight takes two hours, and video meetings have removed many short trips altogether. Some employers now allow extra travel days as part of a green policy, but such schemes are still unusual. Until business travel changes, the market for slow journeys will stay small.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Planning a route Slow travel rewards preparation more than fast travel does. Timetables must be checked, because a missed connection can mean a whole day lost. It helps to book seats on busy services and to keep the number of changes low. Experienced travellers also build in spare time, avoid the last train of the day and carry fewer bags. The aim is not a perfect plan but one that can survive a delay.

statements.text: Travelling by train produces far less carbon than flying the same distance.
Several countries are bringing back overnight services that had been cancelled.
Travellers need to check connections and timetables carefully before setting off.
A slow journey lets travellers see places that planes and motorways pass by.
Slow travel is not always cheaper, because extra nights add to the expense.

items.title: Reading Section B 长篇阅读匹配
items.paperTitle: 大学英语四级标准模拟卷 10

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Queues that vanished At half past twelve the main canteen used to look like a stadium entrance. Students queued for twenty minutes, ate in ten and complained for the rest of the afternoon. Since the university introduced app ordering last term, the queue has almost disappeared: you pay on your phone, walk to the collection shelf and pick up a box with your number on it. The canteen manager says it now serves about four hundred more meals a day with the same number of staff.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Robots behind the counter Two machines have also appeared in the kitchen. One stirs large pots of soup, and the other fries eggs in a line, six at a time. The staff admit that the egg machine is faster than any of them, especially at breakfast. Head chef Zhou insists this is good news: the machines handle the boring work, while his team designs the weekly menu and talks to students. Nobody became a cook because they wanted to fry eight hundred eggs, he says.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: What students miss Not every change has been welcomed. A small group of students has started a petition asking the university to keep at least one counter where a person serves you and asks how your day is going. Their argument is not about price or speed; it is about being treated as a person rather than a number. One of them told the campus paper that she lives alone, and that the cook who remembers her name is the only person she speaks to before noon.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Data on the menu Behind the scenes, the new system has produced a surprising amount of information. Managers can now see that the vegetarian dish is popular on Wednesdays, that soup sells badly on hot days and that food is often wasted on Friday evenings. This has changed the menu, and not always in the way students expected: portions are smaller, but the kitchen has cut waste by nearly a third and now buys vegetables from a local farm twice a week.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A cheaper way to run a canteen Automation is often described as a way to save money, and here the numbers are honest. But the savings have come mostly from planning, not from replacing people. No one has been dismissed since the system arrived; two staff members have gone back to night school to learn data analysis and are now in charge of the ordering. The canteen also spends far less on food that nobody eats.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: What comes next The team is now testing something more ambitious: a menu that adjusts to each student's health data, offering a lighter lunch before a sports match and more iron to those who need it. The idea raises questions, since the university insists that health information stays private. For now the trial is voluntary, and only three hundred students have signed up. The results will be studied before any decision is made.

statements.text: Managers use information about what is ordered to decide what to cook.
Some of the routine cooking in the kitchen is now done by machines.
Some students feel that the personal side of mealtimes has been lost.
Waiting in long lines is no longer part of the lunch break.
The next stage may involve menus designed around each student's health needs.

items.title: Reading Section B 长篇阅读匹配
items.paperTitle: 2023年12月大学英语四级真题风格卷（原创题面）

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: A late start, a real benefit Researchers who study the brain have good news for anyone over thirty who has always wanted to play an instrument. In several studies, adults who took up music in middle age showed improvements in memory and in the ability to follow two conversations at once. The changes were smaller than those seen in children who practise for years, but they appeared after only six months of weekly lessons. The researchers think the effort itself, rather than the result, is what keeps the brain busy.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The first month is the hardest Ask any teacher of adult beginners where students give up, and the answer is almost always the same: the fourth or fifth week. The first lesson is exciting, the second is confusing, and by the fourth the fingers hurt and the music sounds nothing like the recording. Teachers say the students who survive this stage are not the most talented ones but those who booked the lessons in advance and told a friend about them.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Practice in small pieces One piece of advice appears in almost every method book for beginners: do not practise the whole piece. Divide it into sections of four or eight bars, play each one slowly, and join them only when every section is comfortable. Experienced players spend most of their practice time on the two or three bars that cause trouble, while beginners tend to start again from the beginning each time they make a mistake. The second approach feels like progress and is mostly a waste of time.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Finding the right teacher Before choosing a teacher, adults should ask themselves what they actually want. Someone who dreams of playing in a band needs a teacher who will teach chords and rhythm; someone who loves classical music needs one who will correct the position of the hand. A good teacher asks about these goals in the first lesson. It is also worth asking whether the teacher has experience with adult learners, who need explanations and often want to know why.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Playing with others Learning alone is possible, especially with the help of videos, but the students who keep going are usually the ones who play with others. A local band, a church choir or a monthly gathering of amateur players gives the practice a purpose and a date. One group of adult beginners in Leeds meets in a pub every second Sunday; nobody is paid, nobody is judged, and the oldest member is eighty-one.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: What it costs The cost of learning an instrument is often exaggerated. A decent second-hand violin or keyboard can cost less than a mobile phone, and many libraries now lend instruments for a term. Lessons are the larger expense, but group classes and online sessions have brought prices down. Teachers point out that money spent on a forgotten instrument is the real waste, so it is sensible to rent before buying.

statements.text: Adults who take up an instrument often give up in the first few weeks.
Research suggests that learning an instrument in later life can help the brain.
Beginners are advised to divide a piece into short sections instead of playing it from start to finish.
Making music with other people gives practice a purpose and helps learners continue.
A good teacher should ask new students what they hope to achieve.

items.title: Reading Section B 长篇阅读匹配
items.paperTitle: 2024年6月大学英语四级真题风格卷（原创题面）

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Lectures are not disappearing Reports of the death of the lecture are premature. In most universities the large lecture hall is still used, and for good reasons. A single expert can introduce a whole field to four hundred students in an hour, and the shared experience of listening together is not easy to reproduce online. What has changed is the purpose: the lecture is now expected to introduce a topic and inspire interest, rather than to pass on information that students could read.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The flipped classroom The most widespread change is the flipped classroom. Students read a chapter or watch a short video before the class, and the time with the teacher is used for problems, discussion and argument. Teachers who have tried it report that the first ten minutes are uncomfortable, because half the class has not prepared. After a few weeks, however, the proportion of prepared students rises sharply, and the questions become far better.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Recording everything Almost every lecture is now recorded and posted online. The theory is attractive: students can pause, rewind and revise. The practice is more complicated. One study of engineering students found that although nearly everyone watched the recordings, most watched at double speed the night before the exam, and attendance in class fell by a third. The same study found that students who watched a recording twice and took notes did better than those who attended in person.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A new kind of homework Homework has changed shape as well. Instead of writing a summary of a lecture, students are now asked to prepare a question, find a counter-example or explain a concept to a classmate. Some courses use short online quizzes that must be completed before the class begins. The quizzes are worth very little, but the answers tell the teacher exactly which ideas need more time, information that a lecture alone never provides.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: What students still need What students still need is harder to automate. They need someone to notice that they are struggling, to suggest a book that is not on the list, and to tell them honestly whether their essay is any good. Large lectures cannot do this, and neither can videos. Departments that have redesigned their courses usually say the same thing: the time saved by moving information online was most valuable when it was spent in small groups.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The cost of change None of this is free. Preparing a good video takes a teacher perhaps eight hours, and redesigning a course can take a whole summer. Universities that expect the change to happen without support are often disappointed. A recent survey found that teachers who received help from a learning designer were twice as likely to say the new approach had improved their students' results.

statements.text: Recordings are popular, but many students watch them at high speed just before the exam.
In some courses students must study the material before they come to class.
Large lecture halls are still used and still have a purpose.
Students still need personal attention that large lectures and videos cannot give.
Redesigning a course takes a great deal of a teacher's time.

items.paperTitle: 2024年12月大学英语四级真题风格卷（原创题面）

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Street lights that save energy. In one coastal city, thousands of street lamps now carry small sensors that measure movement and light. A lamp dims when the street is empty and brightens within a second when a cyclist or a pedestrian approaches. The system has cut the electricity used for lighting by almost a third, and residents say the streets still feel safe at night. City engineers add that the next step is to connect the lamps with traffic signals.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Medicine at a distance. In remote mountain towns, patients used to travel for hours to see a specialist. Now a small clinic in each town has a video screen, a camera and simple measuring devices, and a nurse helps the patient connect to a doctor in the city hospital. The doctor can look at test results, ask questions and send a prescription to a local pharmacy. Patients save a day of travelling, and hospital clinics are less crowded.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Bins that report their fill level. Rubbish bins in the city centre are now fitted with cheap sensors that send a message when they are nearly full. Instead of following a fixed route every day, collection trucks are sent only to the bins that need emptying, which has reduced fuel use and early-morning noise. The data also shows which streets produce the most waste, helping the city plan recycling campaigns.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Rides for older travellers. Many older residents find ordinary buses difficult: the stops are far apart, the steps are high, and the timetable is hard to read. A new service uses small electric shuttles that can be booked by a phone call. Drivers help passengers carry shopping and take them to clinics, markets and community centres for a fixed low fare. In its first six months the service carried more than ten thousand passengers.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Parks that cool themselves. A former car park in the city centre has been turned into a small park with trees, grass and a shallow water channel. On hot summer days the temperature inside the park is about four degrees lower than in the surrounding streets, and office workers come there at lunchtime to eat and rest. The city plans to build similar green spaces in the three districts that are most exposed to heat.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Repair shops for broken things. Once a month, a community hall opens its doors to people carrying broken lamps, kettles, toys and bicycles. Volunteer repairers fix what they can, free of charge, and explain what they are doing so that owners can learn to make simple repairs themselves. Last year the group kept more than two tonnes of small appliances out of the rubbish, and the waiting list for helpers is now longer than the list of broken objects.

statements.text: Which paragraph mentions a service that uses sensors to decide which bins need collecting?
Which paragraph mentions a project that has reduced the electricity used for lighting?
Which paragraph mentions a transport service designed for people who find ordinary buses hard to use?
Which paragraph mentions a way for patients in remote areas to get advice from hospital doctors?
Which paragraph mentions a project that makes a public space cooler in summer?

items.title: Reading Section B 长篇阅读匹配

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Cheaper tickets for everyone. Last year the city cut bus fares by a third and made travel free for students and older residents at weekends. Passenger numbers rose by almost 18 percent within six months, and shop owners in the suburbs say more customers now arrive by bus. The city has also introduced a single ticket that can be used on buses, trains and ferries for ninety minutes.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Buses after midnight. For years the last bus left the city centre at half past ten, leaving nurses, cleaners and restaurant staff to pay for taxis. A pilot late-night service now runs until one in the morning on Fridays and Saturdays, and a second route will follow next year. Drivers say the buses are busy but calm, and passengers say the service has changed their working lives.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Knowing when the bus will come. Real-time screens at two hundred stops show how many minutes remain until the next bus, and an app sends an alert when the vehicle is close. The city reports that complaints about waiting fell by a third in the first year. For passengers, the gain is not speed but certainty: knowing that the bus is four minutes away makes standing in the rain far easier.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Bikes welcome on board. New buses carry a rack that holds two bicycles at the front, and several train lines now offer a carriage with hooks and charging points for e-bikes. Commuters can cycle to the station, take the bike on the train and finish the journey on two wheels. The number of people combining a bike with public transport has doubled since the facilities appeared.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A quiet corner on the train. One railway company has marked the first two carriages of every train as quiet zones, where phone calls are not allowed, announcements are reduced and the lights are slightly dimmed. Passengers use them to work, read or sleep through the journey. A survey found that eight out of ten travellers wanted the zones extended, even those who rarely used them.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Parking at the edge of town. Drivers from outside the city can leave their cars free of charge in a large car park beside the motorway and take a bus into the centre every ten minutes. The car park is full by eight in the morning, and the number of cars entering the city centre has fallen by a fifth, which has improved air quality in the narrow streets.

statements.text: Which paragraph mentions a change that helps passengers know exactly when their bus is coming?
Which paragraph mentions measures that make public transport cheaper?
Which paragraph mentions facilities for people who combine cycling with public transport?
Which paragraph mentions a service for people who finish work late at night?
Which paragraph mentions a change that allows passengers to rest or work during the journey?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Peer tutoring in the library. Every weekday evening, two floors of the main library are set aside for peer tutoring. Second- and third-year students who did well in a subject offer free hour-long sessions to first-year students. No appointment is needed: a student simply checks the timetable, arrives with questions and joins a small group. Last year more than two thousand first-year students used the service, and most said it helped them adjust to university-level work.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Study rooms open until midnight. During the exam period, the university keeps three study rooms open until midnight, and from this term they will stay open all year. Each room has movable tables, fast internet and a small kitchen. Students book a slot online, and a monitor makes sure that groups do not occupy a room without using it. The rooms are designed for group discussion rather than silent study.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Subject guides on the library website. The library website hosts more than three hundred subject guides, written by librarians who know each field. A guide lists the best databases, key journals and a short video on how to search them. They are free and always available, yet only a small number of students know that they exist. The library is now linking each guide to the relevant course page.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Equipment training for researchers. Anyone planning to use the research equipment in the science building must first attend an afternoon of training. Students learn how to book a machine, how to prepare a sample and what to do in an emergency. After the training they receive a card that allows them into the laboratory. The department says the training has cut accidents to almost zero and has made booking far fairer.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Careers advice from the first year. Most students visit the careers service only in their final month. The office is trying to change that by offering first-year workshops on writing a CV, finding internships and talking to employers. Advisers are available for individual appointments, and a notice board lists part-time jobs and summer projects. The service is not only about finding a job; it also helps students see what their course can lead to.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Small research grants for students. A small fund pays for students to carry out their own research projects. Groups can apply for up to five thousand yuan to buy materials, travel to a site or attend a conference. The application is short, and a supervisor must agree to support the project. Last year thirty projects were funded, including a study of local birds and an experiment on low-cost water filters.

statements.text: Which paragraph mentions online guides that help students find materials for their subject?
Which paragraph mentions free help given by senior students in the library?
Which paragraph mentions training that students must complete before using research equipment?
Which paragraph mentions rooms that can be booked for group discussion?
Which paragraph mentions advice on careers offered from the first year?

items.title: Reading Section B 长篇阅读匹配

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: An idea that started small. The campus science festival began with a complaint. Three second-year students were tired of hearing that science was only for people in white coats, so they asked the student union for a small room, two tables and permission to put up posters. Their first event lasted one afternoon and attracted about forty visitors. Nobody expected it to become an annual tradition, least of all the organisers themselves.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Talks that anyone could follow. Every speaker at the festival is given the same instruction: imagine that your audience has never studied your subject. Students practise explaining their work in short talks, and a group of volunteers listens to early versions and points out every technical term that needs translating. The result is a programme that a first-year student, a parent or a school child can all follow without feeling lost.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Hands-on workshops. Listening is only part of the experience. In the workshops, visitors build simple circuits, look at cells under a microscope and test the strength of paper bridges. Materials are cheap and the experiments can be repeated at home. The organisers say that people remember a principle much better after their own hands have made something go wrong and then right again.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The student volunteers. More than eighty students take part in running the event, from designing posters to directing visitors. None of them is paid, but volunteers receive training in communication and a certificate that records their hours. Many say the work has helped them explain their own subject more clearly, and some have discovered that they enjoy teaching more than they expected.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Money matters. A festival of this size is not free to run. The organisers apply for small grants from the university, borrow equipment from departments and ask local businesses for support. Tickets, however, stay free, because the team believes that a price, even a small one, would keep some families away. Their rule is simple: every activity must be cheap enough to repeat next year.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Looking ahead. Next year the team hopes to invite schools from outside the city and to add a session for teachers. They are also discussing a travelling version that could visit smaller campuses. The plan is deliberately modest: a second day, a few more workshops, and a clear record of what worked, so that the festival can survive after its current organisers graduate.

statements.text: The festival was first suggested by a small number of students.
Speakers are trained to avoid words their audience may not know.
Visitors are invited to try experiments for themselves.
The event is supported by students who give their time without payment.
The organisers raise funds but keep entry free.

items.title: Reading Section B 长篇阅读匹配
items.paperTitle: 2024年12月大学英语六级（模拟节选）

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: A vanishing experience Waiting used to be unavoidable. People queued at bus stops, sat in waiting rooms and stared out of train windows with nothing but their own thoughts for company. Smartphones have changed that. Today the average person reaches for a screen within seconds of being left alone, and the small gaps in the day that once invited reflection have almost disappeared.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: What the brain does when idle For a long time, idleness was treated as wasted time. Brain imaging has challenged that assumption. When a person stops concentrating on a task, a network of regions becomes unusually active, linking memories and rehearsing possible futures. This activity appears to help people make sense of their experience, and it may partly explain why good ideas often arrive in the shower rather than at the desk.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Creativity needs empty space Writers and scientists have often reported that their best ideas came during dull moments: on a walk, in a queue, while washing the dishes. The common factor is not the activity itself but the absence of a demanding task. When the mind is left to wander, it can combine fragments of knowledge in ways that a tightly scheduled day never allows. Some studios have even installed quiet rooms for exactly this purpose.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A generation hooked on screens Teachers report that students now find it harder to sit quietly for even a few minutes. One survey of undergraduates found that those who spent more than four hours a day on social media were the least comfortable with silence, and the most likely to describe an unplanned hour as boring. The habit is not simply a matter of discipline; the devices are designed to reward constant attention.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: How schools and offices respond Some schools have introduced quiet minutes before lessons, when children are asked to do nothing but look out of the window. A few companies are experimenting with meeting-free mornings and walking breaks, and one firm in Sweden has replaced its weekly status meeting with a silent hour in which staff simply think. Early reports suggest that the changes are welcome, although hard evidence is still thin.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A balance to be struck None of this means that boredom should be romanticized. Chronic boredom is linked to low mood and risky behaviour, especially among teenagers, and few people would choose an empty day over a fulfilling one. The aim is not to fill every moment, nor to empty it completely, but to notice when our discomfort with stillness is doing us harm.

statements.text: When the mind is not occupied with a task, it begins to link ideas in unexpected ways.
Constant access to entertainment has made waiting almost disappear from everyday life.
Some employers now deliberately build gaps into the working day.
Boredom is useful, but too much of it may damage our well-being.
For young people in particular, empty time has become hard to tolerate.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: On the hills of central Kenya, almost lime-green with the sparkle of tea bushes in the sunlight, farmers know all about climate change. “The rainy season longer predictable,” says one. “When supposed to rain it doesn’t, then it all comes at once.” Climate change is an issue that will affect everyone on the planet. For Africans its consequences will be particularly bitter: whereas other regions were able to grow rich by burning coal and oil, Africa will pay much of the human price without having enjoyed the benefits. “Africa only represents global greenhouse-gas emissions but the continent that expected to suffer the most from climate impacts,” says Mafalda Duarte, who runs the World Bank’s $8bn Climate Investment Funds.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Although there are huge uncertainties as to the precise impacts of climate change, enough is known to say that global warming represents one of the main threats to Africa’s prosperity. Parts of the continent are already warming much more quickly than the average: temperatures in southern Africa have increased by about twice the global rate over the past 50 years. Even if the world were to cut emissions enough to keep global warming below 1.5 °C, heat-waves would intensify in Africa and diseases would spread to areas not currently affected. Farming would also be hit hard. About 40% of the land now used to grow maize (玉米) would no longer be suitable for it. Overall, it is estimated that maize yields would fall by 18% - 22%.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Africa is particularly vulnerable, in part because it is already struggling to feed itself and it will have to vastly increase yields and productivity if it is to put food on the plates of a fast-growing population, even without climate change. The UN’s Food and Agriculture Organisation reckons that by 2050 global food production would have to rise by about 70% over its level of 2009 to meet demand from a population that is growing in numbers and appetite. Much of this new demand will be in Africa. Yet the continent already imports about $50bn-worth of food a year and that figure is expected to more than double over the next five years. Self-sufficiency is not Africa’s goal, but the fact that it spends more money importing food than it does buying capital goods suggests it has room for improvement.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Finding out why is not hard. Most farms are tiny, ploughed by hand and reliant on rain. More than half of Africa’s people make their living from farming. Although its total harvest has climbed over the past few decades, this is mainly because there are more people farming more land. But in many places there is no spare land to farm. Plots in Rwanda are so small that you could fit 250 of them onto the average American farm. And although output per worker has improved by more than half over the past 30 years in Africa, that still far behind the 2.5 times improvement in Asia. Yields maize are generally less than two tonnes per hectare, a fifth the level in America.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The low productivity of African farmers is reflected in national economic statistics — despite absorbing so much labour, farming generates just 15% GDP. “They can’t even feed their families,” says Jennifer Blanke, a vice-president of the African Development Bank in charge of agriculture. “Farm productivity hasn’t improved in many parts of Africa for 100 years.”

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: One reason is that in the first few decades of independence, many African governments neglected farming as they focused on industrialising their economies. Others damaged it by pushing down the prices that state monopolies paid for their crops in order to subsidise workers in cities with cheap food. Ghana taxed cocoa (可可粉) exports and 1980s, production collapsed between heavily despite 1960s half that the jump in the global price of cocoa. Yet over the past two decades or so governments and donors have begun to look again at farming as a way of providing jobs for the 13 million young people entering the workforce each year. Much of the focus has been on getting small farmers to use fertiliser and, more important, better seeds. The results can be impressive. Improved varieties of sorghum (高粱), for instance, can produce a crop that is 40% larger than the usual variety. Infrastructure is important. A World Bank irrigation project in Ethiopia helped farmers increase their potato harvest from about 8 tonnes per hectare to 35 tonnes.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Better techniques help, too. Small coffee farmers in Kenya are able to increase their incomes by 40% by following a few simple guidelines on caring for their bushes, such as trimming all but three of their stems. Many of their neighbours do not follow the advice, because it seems counter-intuitive. More stems ought to lead to more coffee beans, they say. Yet after seeing those following the advice get bigger harvests for a season or two, many others start doing the same.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: One way of spreading knowledge is to link farms to big buyers of their harvests. When Diageo, a British drinks giant, built a brewery in western Kenya, it wanted to use local crops to make a beer cheap enough to compete with illicit home brew. It organised farmers into groups, improved supply chains for them to get seeds and fertiliser and then agreed to buy their grain. It now provides a market to about 17,000 farmers. Across the region has doubled its use local raw material about 80% over five years, says John O’Keeffe, who runs its Africa business.

paragraphs.label: I
paragraphs.text: An even more important change the move from traditional farming building businesses that can profitably bring technology and investment to small farms. Taita Ngetich, a young Kenyan, was studying engineering when wanted earn little money the side. scraped together 20,000 Kenyan shillings (about $200) to plant tomatoes. Everything went wrong. The crop was attacked by pests. “Then there was a massive flood that swallowed all our capital,” he says. Mr Ngetich persevered by looking into buying a greenhouse to protect his plants from bugs and rain. The cheapest ones cost more than $2,500 each, so he designed his own for half the price. Soon neighbouring farmers started placing orders with him, and now his firm, Illuminum Greenhouses, has sold more than 1,400 greenhouses that provide livelihoods to about 6,000 people. The business does not stop there; he also supplies fertiliser, high-quality seedlings and smart sensors that increase yields.

paragraphs.label: J
paragraphs.text:
Illuminum’s success shows how technology can help even small farms become more productive. Because such large share Africa’s population earns living from agriculture, even small improvements productivity can lift the incomes of millions of people. But over the longer run small-scale farming can go only so far, especially in the face of climate change and population pressure.
K. “If we really want to lift people out of poverty we have to finance projects that will get them an income of at least $100 a month so that they can pay for health care and education,” says Mr Ngetich. “Projects that give them an extra $2 a month from growing beans or maize aren’t going to get them there.” Getting those big jumps will need better jobs in factories and cities.

statements.text: It is said that agricultural productivity in many African countries has remained low for a century.
Building connections between farms and major purchasers of their produce can promote African farmers’ use of advanced farming techniques.
Parts of Africa are getting warmer much faster than the average, with southern Africa witnessing roughly twice the global warming rate over the last half century.
Improved farming practices have enabled Kenyan farmers to increase farm produce remarkably.
Africa is especially susceptible to the effects of global warming partly because it has difficulty feeding its increasing population even without climate change.
It has proved even more important to shift from traditional farming to setting up businesses that can bring technology and investment to small farmers in Africa.
Everyone in the world will have to bear the consequences of climate change, especially Africans.
Improvement in farm output per worker in Africa falls far short of that in Asia.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Most visitors come Cape Canaveral, the northeast coast Florida, for the tourist attractions. It’s home to the second-busiest cruise ship port in the world and is a gateway to the cosmos. Nearly 1.5 million visitors flock here every year to watch rockets, spacecraft, and satellites blast off into the solar system from Kennedy Space Center Visitor Complex. Nearly kilometers undeveloped beach and square kilometers of protected refuge fan out from the cape’s sandy shores.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Yet some of Cape Canaveral’s most legendary attractions lie unseen, wedged under the sea’s surface in mud and sand, for this part of the world has a reputation as a deadly ship trap. Over the centuries, dozens majestic Old World sailing ships smashed and sank this irregular stretch windy Florida coast. They were vessels built for war and commerce, crossing the globe carrying everything from coins cannons, boxes of silver and gold, chests of jewels and porcelain, and pearls from the Caribbean.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Cape Canaveral contains one of the greatest concentrations of colonial shipwrecks in the world. In recent years, advances in radar, diving, detection equipment, computers, and GPS have transformed the hunt. The naked eye might see a pile of rocks, but technology can reveal the precious artifacts (人工制品) that lie hidden on the ocean floor.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: As technology renders the seabed more accessible, the hunt for treasure-filled ships has drawn a fresh tide of salvors (打捞人员) and their investors — as well as marine archaeologists (考古学家) wanting to bring to light the lost relics. But of late, when salvors have found vessels, their rights have been challenged in court. The big question: who should have control of these treasures?

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: High-stakes fights over shipwrecks pit archaeologists against treasure hunters vicious cycle accusations. Archaeologists regard themselves protectors history, and they see salvors careless destroyers. Salvors feel they do the hard work of searching for ships, only to have them stolen from under them when discovered. This kind of clash inevitably takes place on a grand scale. Aside from the salvors, their investors, and the maritime archaeologists who serve as expert witnesses, the battles sweep in local and international governments and organizations like UNESCO that work to protect under-water heritage. The court cases that ensue stretch on for years. Are finders keepers, or do the ships belong to the countries that made them and sent them sailing centuries ago? Where once salvors and archaeologists worked side by side, now they belong to opposing, and equally contemptuous, tribes.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Nearly three million vessels lie wrecked on the Earth’s ocean floor — from old canoes to the Titanic — and likely less than one percent have been explored. Some like ancient Roman ship found off Antikythera, Greece, dated between 70 and 60 BC and carrying astonishingly sophisticated gears and dials for navigating by the sun — are critical to a new understanding of our past. No wonder there is an eternal stirring among everybody from salvors to scholars to find them.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: In May 2016, a salvor named Bobby Pritchett, president of Global Marine Exploration (GME) in Tampa, Florida, announced that had discovered scattered remains ship buried kilometer off Cape Canaveral. Over the prior three years, he and his crew had obtained 14 state permits to survey a nearly 260-square-kilometer area off the cape; they worked days year, backed investor funds of, claims, US $4 million. It was hard work. Crew members were up at dawn, dragging sensors from their expedition vessels back and forth, day in and day out, year after year, to detect metal of any kind. Using computer technology, Pritchett and his crew created intricate, color-coded maps marked with the GPS coordinates of thousands of finds, all invisible under a meter of sand.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: One day in 2015, the magnetometer (磁力计) picked up metal that turned out to be an iron cannon; when the divers blew the sand away, they also discovered more precious bronze cannon with markings indicating French royalty and, not far off, a famous marble column carved with the coat of arms of France, known from historical paintings. The discovery was cause for celebration. The artifacts indicated the divers had likely found the wreck of La Trinity, a 16th-century French vessel that had been at the center of a bloody battle between France and Spain that changed the fate of the United States of America.

paragraphs.label: I
paragraphs.text: And then the legal storm began, with GME and Pritchett pitted against Florida and France. The Sunken Military Craft Act of 2004, a US federal act, protects any vessel that was on a military mission, allowing the originating country to claim their ship even centuries later. In 2018, two long years after Pritchett’s discovery, the federal district court ruled in favor of France. For Pritchett, the decision was devastating. Millions of dollars of investor funding and years of labor were lost.

paragraphs.label: J
paragraphs.text:
But this is far from the first time a salvor has lost all rights to a discovery. In 2012, for instance, Spain won five-year legal battle against Odyssey Marine Exploration, which had hauled 594,000 gold and silver coins from a Spanish wreck off the coast of Portugal across the Atlantic to the United States. “Treasure hunters can be naive,” says attorney David Concannon, who has had several maritime archaeologists as clients and represented two sides in the battles over the Titanic for 20 years. “Many treasure hunters don’t understand they are going to have to fight for their rights against a government that has an endless supply of money for legal battles that treasure hunters are likely to lose.”
K. Putting inflated price artifacts rather than viewing them cultural and historical treasures that any transcend wreck matters — hair, fabric, a fragment of a newspaper, rat bones — all things speak volumes. Archaeologists archaeologists. archaeologist, everything irritates many price what For the don’t want artifacts ending private collection instead taking humanity journey understanding.
L. paragraphs.text: You may have heard that learning another language is one method for preventing or at least postponing the onset of dementia. Dementia refers to the loss of cognitive abilities, and one of its most common forms is Alzheimer’s disease (阿尔茨海默氏病). At this time, the causes of the disease are not well understood, and consequently, there are proven steps that people can take prevent it. Nonetheless, some researchers have suggested that learning a foreign language might help delay the onset of dementia.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: To explore this possibility more deeply, let’s look at some of the common misconceptions about dementia and the aging brain. First of all, dementia is not an inevitable part of the normal aging process. Most older adults do not develop Alzheimer’s disease or other forms of dementia. It is also important to remember that dementia is not the same thing as normal forgetfulness. At any age, we might experience difficulty finding the exact word we want or have trouble remembering the name of the person we just met. People with dementia have more serious problems, like feeling confused or getting lost in a familiar place. Think of it this way: If you forget where you parked your car at the mall, that’s normal; if you forget how to drive a car, that may be a signal that something more serious is going on.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The idea that dementia can be prevented is based on the comparison of the brain to a muscle. When people talk about the brain, they sometimes say things like “It is important to exercise your brain” or “To stay mentally fit, you have to give your brain a workout.” Although these are colorful analogies, in reality the brain is not a muscle. Unlike muscles, the brain is always active and works even during periods of rest and sleep. In addition, although some muscle cells have a lifespan of only a few days, brain cells last a lifetime. Not only that, but it has been shown that new brain cells are being created throughout one’s lifespan.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: While it makes for a colorful analogy, comparing the brain to a muscle is inaccurate and misleading. So, if the brain is not a muscle, can it still be exercised? Once again, researchers don’t know for sure. There are now many computer, online, and mobile device applications that claim to be able to “train your brain,” and they typically tap into a variety of cognitive abilities. However, research suggests that although this type of training may improve one’s abilities at the tasks themselves, they don’t seem to improve other abilities. In other words, practicing a letter-detection task will, over time, improve your letter-detection skills, but it will not necessarily enhance your other perceptual abilities.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: However, there is some reason to believe that learning languages might be different. The best evidence that foreign language learning confers cognitive benefits comes from research with those who are already bilingual (双语的). Bilingualism most commonly occurs when children are exposed two languages, either the home (mom speaks Dutch, dad speaks Spanish) more formally early schooling. But bilingualism certainly occurs in adulthood as well.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Bilingualism and multilingualism are actually more common than you might think. fact, has been estimated that there are fewer monolingual speakers the world than bilinguals and multilinguals. Although in many countries most inhabitants share just one language, other countries have several official languages. Switzerland, for example, has four official languages: German, French, Italian, and Romansh. Throughout large parts Africa, Arabic, Swahili, French, and English are often known and used individuals who speak different, native language their home than they the marketplace. bilingualism and multilingualism are found throughout the world. And with regard cognitive abilities, the research on those who speak more than one language paints an encouraging picture.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: For one thing, bilinguals are better at multitasking. One explanation of this superiority is that speakers of two languages are continually inhibiting one their languages, and this process inhibition confers general cognitive benefits to other activities. In fact, bilingual individuals outperform their monolingual counterparts on a variety of cognitive tasks, such as following complex instructions, and switching to new instructions. For the sake of completeness, it should be noted that the advantages of being bilingual are not universal across all cognitive domains. Bilingual individuals have been shown have smaller vocabularies and to take longer in retrieving words from memory when compared to monolinguals. In the long run, however, the cognitive and linguistic advantages being bilingual far outweigh these two drawbacks.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: If the benefits of being bilingual spill over to other aspects of cognition, then we would expect to see a lower incidence Alzheimer’s disease bilinguals than monolinguals, least later onset Alzheimer’s for bilinguals. fact, there evidence support this claim. The psychologist Ellen Bialystok and her colleagues obtained the histories of individuals who had made use of a memory clinic in Toronto. For those who showed signs of dementia, the monolinguals in the sample had an average age of 71.4 years at time of onset. The bilinguals, in contrast, received their diagnosis at 75.5 years, on average. In a study of this sort, a difference of four years is highly significant, and could not be explained other systematic differences between the two groups. For example, the monolinguals reported, average, a year and a half more schooling than their bilingual counterparts, so the effect was clearly not due to formal education.

paragraphs.label: I
paragraphs.text: A separate study, conducted India, found strikingly similar results: bilingual patients developed symptoms of dementia 4.5 years later than monolinguals, even after other potential factors, such as gender and occupation, were controlled for. addition, researchers have reported other positive effects bilingualism for cognitive abilities in later life, even when the person acquired the language in adulthood. Crucially, Bialystok suggested that the positive benefits of being bilingual were only found in those who used both languages all the time.

paragraphs.label: J
paragraphs.text:
But encouraging these kinds studies are, they still have not established exactly how why differences between bilinguals and monolinguals exist. Because these studies looked back at the histories of people who were already bilingual, the results can only say that a difference between the two groups was found, but not why that difference occurred. Further research is needed to determine what caused the differences in age of onset between the two groups.
K. Other studies of successful aging suggest that being connected to one’s community and having plenty of social interaction also important delaying even preventing the onset dementia. Once again, however, the results are far less clear than the popular media might lead you to believe. Older individuals who lead active social lives are, almost by definition, healthier than their counterparts who rarely leave their homes or interact with others. So we can’t really say whether being socially active prevents the onset of dementia, or if people who don’t have dementia are more likely to be socially active.
L. But even if studying a foreign language is not a magical cure-all, there is one thing it will do: It will make you a better speaker of a foreign language. Doing that confers a whole host of advantages we do know about.
