paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: I can be a reluctant socialiser. I’m sometimes secretly pleased when social plans are called off. I get restless a few hours into a hangout. I even once went on a free 10-day silent meditation (冥想) retreat — not for the meditation, The Benefits of Solitude but for the silence.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: So I can relate to author Anneli Rufus, who wrote in Party of One: The Loners’ Manifesto: “When parents on TV shows punished their kids by ordering them to go to their rooms, I was confused. I loved my room. Being there behind a locked door was a treat. To me a punishment was being ordered to play games with my cousin Louis.”

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Unsocial tendencies like these are often far from ideal. Abundant research shows the harms of social isolation, considered a serious public health problem in countries that have rapidly ageing populations (though talk of a ‘loneliness epidemic’ may exaggerated). the UK, the Royal College General Practitioners says that loneliness has the same risk level for premature death as diabetes. Strong social connections are important for cognitive functioning, motor function and a smoothly running immune system.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: This is especially clear from cases of extreme social isolation. Examples of people kept in captivity, children kept isolated in abusive orphanages, and prisoners kept in solitary confinement all show how prolonged solitude can lead to hallucinations (幻觉) and other forms of mental instability.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: But these are severe and involuntary cases of aloneness. For those of us who just prefer plenty of alone time, emerging research suggests some good news: there are upsides to being alone — for both our work lives and our emotional well-being.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Solitude is a time for reflection, for thinking about things more deeply. In a world increasingly focused on speed and competitiveness, solitude is precious and something to be treasured. And there are benefits in learning to love your solitude.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: One key benefit of solitude is improved creativity. Gregory Feist, who focuses on the psychology of creativity at California’s San Jose State University, has defined creativity thinking activity with two key elements: originality and usefulness. He has found that personality traits commonly associated with creativity are openness (receptiveness to new thoughts and experiences), self-confidence, and autonomy — which may include “a lack of concern for social norms” and “a preference for being alone”. In fact, Feist’s research on both artists and scientists shows that one of the most prominent features of creative folks is their lesser interest in socialising.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: One reason for this is that such people are likely to spend sustained time alone working on their craft. Plus, Feist says, many artists “are trying to make sense of their internal world and a lot of internal personal experiences that they’re trying give expression and meaning through their art.” Solitude allows for the reflection and observation necessary for that creative process.

paragraphs.label: I
paragraphs.text: A recent justification of these ideas came from University at Buffalo psychologist Julie Bowker, who researches social withdrawal. Social withdrawal is usually categorised into three types: shyness caused by fear or anxiety; avoidance, from a dislike of socialising; and unsociability, from a preference for solitude. A paper by Bowker and her colleagues was the first to show that a type of social withdrawal could have a positive effect — they found that creativity was linked specifically to unsociability. They also found that unsociability had no correlation with aggression (shyness and avoidance did). This was significant because while previous research had suggested that unsociability might harmless, Bowker and colleagues’ paper showed that could actually beneficial. Unsociable people are likely to be “having just enough interaction,” Bowker says. “They have a preference for being alone, but they also don’t mind being with others.”

paragraphs.label: J
paragraphs.text:
Still, it turns out that solitude is important for more than creativity. It’s commonly believed that leaders need to be sociable. But this depends, among other things, on the personalities of their employees. One 2011 study showed that branches pizza chain where employees were more passive, outgoing were associated with higher profits. But branches where employees were more active, introverted leaders were more bosses ( 内向 的) effective. One reason for this is that introverted people are less likely to feel threatened by strong personalities and suggestions. They’re also more likely to listen.
K. Since ancient times, meanwhile, people have been aware of a link between isolation and mental focus. After all, cultures with traditions of religious hermits (隐士) believe that solitude is important for enlightenment. Recent research has given us a better understanding of why. One benefit of unsociability is the brain’s state of active mental rest, which goes hand-in-hand with the stillness of being alone. When another person is present, your brain can’t help but pay some attention. This can be a positive distraction. But it’s still a distraction.
L. Daydreaming the absence such distractions activates the brain’s default-mode network. Among other functions, this network helps consolidate memory and understand others’ emotions. Giving free rein wandering mind not only helps with focus in the long term but strengthens your sense of both yourself and others. Paradoxically, therefore, periods of solitude actually help when it comes time to socialise once more. And the occasional absence of focus ultimately helps concentration in the long run.
M. A more recent advocate thoughtful and productive solitude Susan Cain, author Quiet: The Power Introverts in a World That Can’t Stop Talking and founder of Quiet Revolution, a company that promotes quiet and introvert-friendly workplaces. “These days, tend believe that creativity emerges from decidedly unreserved socialising process, but in fact it requires sustained attention and deep focus,” she says. “Also, humans are such absorbent social beings that when surround ourselves with others, automatically take their opinions and aesthetics. To truly chart our own path or vision, we have to be willing to isolate ourselves, at least for some period of time.”
N. Still, the line between useful solitude and dangerous isolation can be blurry. “Almost anything can be adaptive and maladaptive, depending how extreme they get,” Feist says. disorder has with dysfunction. someone stops caring about people and cuts off all contact, this could point irrational neglect social relations. But creative unsociability is a far cry from this. In fact, Feist says, “there’s a real danger with people who are never alone.” It’s hard to examine one’s own thoughts, feelings and motives, to be self-aware, and fully relaxed unless you have occasional solitude. In addition, introverts tend to have fewer but stronger friendships — which has been linked to greater happiness. O. As with many things, quality reigns over quantity. Nurturing a few solid relationships without feeling the need to constantly populate your life with endless chatting ultimately may be better for you. P. Thus, if your personality tends toward unsociability, you shouldn’t feel the need to change. Of course, that comes with qualifications. But as long as you have regular social contact, you are choosing solitude rather than being forced into it, you have at least a few good friends and your solitude is good for your well-being or productivity, there’s no point agonising over how to fit a square personality into a round hole.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: As the scale and impacts of climate change become increasingly alarming, meat is a popular target for action. Advocates for the protection of the natural environment from destruction or pollution urge the public to eat less meat. Some activists have even called for taxing meat to reduce consumption of it.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: A key claim underlying these arguments holds that globally, meat production generates more greenhouse gases than the entire transportation sector. However, this claim demonstrably wrong, will show. And its persistence has led to false assumptions about the linkage between meat and climate change.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: My recent research focuses on ways in which animal agriculture affects air quality and climate change. In my view, there are many reasons for either choosing animal protein or opting for a vegetarian selection. However, abandoning meat and meat products is not the environmental panacea (万灵药) many would have us believe. And if taken to an extreme, it also could have harmful nutritional consequences.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A healthy portion meat’s negative reputation centers the assertion that livestock the largest source greenhouse gases worldwide. For example, an analysis published in 2009 by the World Watch Institute based in Washington, D.C. asserted that 51 percent of global greenhouse gas emissions come from rearing and processing livestock. According the Environmental Protection Agency, the largest sources greenhouse gas emissions were electricity production (28 percent total emissions), transportation (28 percent) and industry (22 percent). All of agriculture accounted for a total of 9 percent, but all of animal agriculture contributes less than half of this amount, representing 3.9 percent of the total greenhouse emission in the US. That is very different from claiming that livestock represents as much as or more than transportation.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Why there such misconception? the United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) published a study titled “Livestock’s Long Shadow,” which received widespread international attention. It stated that livestock produced staggering percent the world’s greenhouse gas emissions. The agency drew startling conclusion that livestock was doing more to harm the climate than all modes of transportation combined. This latter claim was wrong, and has since been corrected by Henning Stenfeld, the report’s senior author.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The problem was that analysts from the FAO used a comprehensive life-cycle assessment to study the climate impact livestock, but different method when they analyzed transportation. For livestock, they considered every factor associated with producing meat. This included emissions from fertilizer production, converting land from forests to pastures, growing feed, and direct emissions from animals (manure as well as expelling of gas from the stomach) from birth to death.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: However, when they looked transportation’s carbon footprint, they ignored impacts the climate from manufacturing vehicle materials and parts, assembling vehicles and maintaining roads, bridges and airports. Instead, they only considered the exhaust smoke emitted by finished cars, trucks, trains and planes. As a result, the FAO’s comparison greenhouse gas emissions from livestock those from transportation was greatly distorted.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: I pointed out this flaw during a speech to fellow scientists in San Francisco on March 22, 2010, which led to a flood of media coverage. To its credit, the FAO immediately owned up to its error. Unfortunately, the agency’s initial claim that livestock was responsible for the lion’s share of world greenhouse gas emissions had already received wide coverage. To this day, we struggle to “unring” the bell. In its most recent assessment report, the FAO estimated that livestock produces 14.5 percent of global greenhouse gas emissions from human activities. There is no comparable full life-cycle assessment for transportation. However, as Stenfeld has pointed out, direct emissions from transportation versus livestock can be compared and amount to 14 versus 5 percent, respectively.

paragraphs.label: I
paragraphs.text: Many people continue think that avoiding meat infrequently once week will make significant difference to the climate. But according to one recent study, even if Americans eliminated all animal protein from their diets, they would reduce US greenhouse gas emissions by only 2.6 percent. According to our research at the University of California, Davis, if the practice of Meatless Monday were to be adopted by all Americans, we’d see a reduction of only 0.5 percent.

paragraphs.label: J
paragraphs.text:
Moreover, technological, genetic and management changes that have taken place in US agriculture over the past years have made livestock production more efficient and less greenhouse gas-intensive. According the FAO’s statistical database, total direct greenhouse gas emissions from US livestock have declined by 11.3 percent since 1961, while production of livestock meat has more than doubled.
K. Demand for meat is rising in developing and emerging economies, especially in the Middle East, North Africa and Southeast Asia. For example, raising livestock such as goats in Kenya is an important source of food and income for many small-scale farmers and herders. But meat consumption per person in these regions still lags that developed countries. In 2015, average annual meat consumption per person developed countries was kilograms, compared to 24 kilograms in the Middle East and North Africa and 18 kilograms in Southeast Asia. Still, given projected population growth the developing world, there will certainly opportunity for countries such as the United States to bring their sustainable livestock rearing practices to the table.
L. Removing animals from US agriculture would lower national greenhouse gas emissions to a small degree, but it would also make it harder to meet people’s nutritional requirements. Many critics of animal agriculture are quick to point out that if farmers raised only plants, they could produce more pounds of food and more calories per person. But humans also need many essential micro- and macro-nutrients for good health. It’s hard to make a compelling argument that the United States has a calorie deficit, given its high national rates of adult and child obesity. Moreover, not all plant parts are edible or desirable. Raising livestock is a way to add nutritional and economic value to plant agriculture.
M. As one example, the energy in plants that livestock consume is most often contained in cellulose (纤维素), which is indigestible for humans and many other mammals. But cows, sheep and other ruminant (反刍的) animals can break cellulose down and release the solar energy contained in this vast resource. According to the FAO, as much as 70 percent of all agricultural land globally is range land that can only be utilized as grazing land for ruminant livestock.
N. The world population is currently projected to reach 9.8 billion by 2050. Feeding this many people will raise immense challenges. Meat more calorie-dense per serving than vegetarian options, and ruminant animals largely thrive on feed that is not suitable for humans. Raising livestock also offers much-needed income for small- scale farmers in developing nations. Worldwide, livestock provides a livelihood for 1 billion people. O. Climate change demands urgent attention, and the livestock industry has a large overall environmental footprint that affects air, water and land. These, combined with rapidly rising world population, give plenty compelling reasons to continue to work for greater efficiencies in animal agriculture. I believe the place to start is with science-based facts.

statements.text: The FAO concluded that farm animals were producing more greenhouse gases than all modes of transportation combined.
Consumption of meat per person in developing countries is much less than that in countries like the US.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Buying used goods once carried a faint smell of hardship. Today the same act is presented as clever, thrifty and even stylish. Influential voices online show off furniture rescued from skips and coats found in charity shops, and their audiences copy the behaviour. The shift is partly economic and partly cultural: people want their purchases to say something about their values as well as their taste. Parents who once hid a second-hand purchase now mention it proudly. As a result, a market that was once hidden at the edge of town has moved into the mainstream.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The environmental argument is straightforward. Every object that changes hands a second time is an object that does not have to be manufactured, shipped and eventually buried. That saves materials, energy and space in landfill. Campaigners point out that the greenest item is usually the one already in existence, and that buying nothing new is more effective than buying something labelled sustainable. For a generation worried about waste, this logic is difficult to argue with. The calculation differs from person to person, but the direction is the same.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Second-hand shopping requires a different kind of attention. A buyer cannot assume that a coat has been cleaned or that a chair has all its legs. Photographs may hide stains, and a description that sounds enthusiastic may omit a fault. Experienced shoppers inspect seams, ask about measurements and request extra images before they commit. They also learn to walk away from a bargain that will cost more to repair than to replace. A little patience saves both money and disappointment.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Online platforms have solved the trust problem in a simple way: they let strangers rate each other. A seller with hundreds of positive reviews is unlikely to risk a bad one for a small gain, and buyers who feel cheated can warn others. Some sites hold the payment until the item arrives, which removes the fear of paying for nothing. These small mechanisms have made it normal to send money to somebody you have never met. Reputation, in other words, has replaced the handshake.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: For many sellers the motivation is not money but space. A flat fills up with clothes that no longer fit and gadgets that were used twice, and throwing them away feels wasteful. Listing an item takes minutes, and the buyer often collects it from the doorstep. The result is a home that feels lighter and a small sum that appears in the bank. Sellers describe the process as a form of tidying that pays for itself. Some describe selling as a way of learning what they never use.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Older objects have an advantage that new ones often lack. Furniture built decades ago was frequently made from solid wood and designed to be mended, while a cheap modern equivalent may be glued together and impossible to repair. Collectors seek out such pieces for their materials and their character, and some manufacturers have noticed, reissuing classic designs or emphasising durability in their marketing. The appeal is not only nostalgia; it is also a judgement about quality that buyers can test with their hands.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The risks are real. Counterfeit goods, stolen bicycles and items that arrive broken are all part of the picture. Most platforms offer some protection, but a buyer who pays in cash on a doorstep has little recourse. Consumer groups advise meeting in public places, keeping a record of the conversation, and checking serial numbers where possible. They also warn that a price far below the market rate is usually a warning sign. Vigilance, rather than trust, is the price of a good bargain.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: Retailers have responded not by fighting the trend but by joining it. Several chains now buy back worn clothing and resell it, and electronics shops offer trade-in credit against a new purchase. The motive is partly ethical and partly commercial: a customer who returns to sell is a customer who may also buy. For the shops, the second-hand section attracts people who would otherwise never enter the store. For them the used rail is less a threat than an extra shop window.

paragraphs.label: I
paragraphs.text: Clothing shows the pattern most clearly. Fashion cycles now move quickly, and garments are often worn a few times before losing their appeal. Resale gives them a second life and gives buyers a way to follow trends without paying full price. Some young shoppers build whole wardrobes from used items and treat the hunt as entertainment. Critics worry that this simply speeds up consumption rather than reducing it. The industry has noticed, and some labels now design clothes with resale in mind.

paragraphs.label: J
paragraphs.text: Lawmakers are beginning to catch up. Rules that once applied only to shops are being extended to individuals who sell regularly, and platforms are expected to check that goods are not stolen. Consumer protection bodies want the same guarantees for used products that new ones receive. Sellers complain about paperwork, but the direction of travel is clear: the second-hand market is no longer a private arrangement between neighbours. What was once a favour between friends is becoming a market with obligations.

statements.text: Buying second-hand is now treated as a smart and principled choice rather than a sign of poverty.
Choosing an object that already exists is greener than buying a new one marketed as sustainable.
Used goods demand close inspection because sellers may not mention every defect.
Reputation scores and delayed payment let strangers trade safely without meeting.
Many people sell mainly to clear space and feel better about their homes.
Well-made old furniture is prized because cheap modern versions cannot be repaired.
Shoppers are warned about unusually low prices and advised to keep evidence.
Established shops join resale because it brings in people who rarely visit.
Fast fashion drives resale while also raising doubts about total consumption.
Rules once aimed at businesses are being applied to frequent individual sellers.

items.title: Hiring for Skill, Not for Talk

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: The traditional job interview is a conversation between strangers, and it is a poor predictor of how someone will actually work. Candidates who are charming and fluent often impress an interviewer without demonstrating any relevant ability, while quieter applicants with stronger skills may be overlooked. Employers have long known this, but the interview survived because it was cheap and familiar. Now that hiring is expensive and mistakes are visible, more companies are looking for evidence rather than impressions. The cost of a poor appointment is easier to notice than the weakness of the conversation that led to it.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most direct alternative is a work sample. A designer is asked to redesign a page, an analyst to interpret a small dataset, and a customer service candidate to answer a set of realistic complaints. Because the task resembles the job, performance on it tells an employer something that no conversation can. Candidates generally prefer this too: a practical test feels fairer than being judged on small talk and a firm handshake. Employers also find that a task reveals how a person handles instructions and deadlines.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Practical hiring can widen the pool of applicants. A person without a degree may still write excellent code or manage a project calmly, and a test allows that ability to surface. Employers who drop formal qualification requirements often report a larger and more varied set of candidates. For workers who learned their trade outside universities, this is a rare route past a filter that would otherwise reject them before any human being reads their name. A test, unlike a degree, can be designed around the actual work rather than around a syllabus.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: There is a catch. A take-home task can amount to hours of unpaid work, and candidates with caring responsibilities cannot always spare an evening. Some firms have responded by keeping tasks short, paying a small fee, or running the exercise during a scheduled session. Without such safeguards, a method that looks objective may simply reward people with free time, which is a poor proxy for talent. The fairness of the process, not its sophistication, decides whether candidates trust it.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Skills-based hiring also changes how existing staff are treated. Instead of relying on job titles, an organisation can assess what employees can actually do and move them into roles where those abilities are needed. This is popular with workers who feel stuck in a department because their formal qualifications do not match a vacancy. It also helps employers fill gaps internally when the external market is thin. The result is a workforce that can be redeployed instead of replaced.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The approach only works if the people doing the assessing are trained. An untrained interviewer may favour a candidate who reminds them of themselves, or may mark an unusual but effective solution as wrong. Good practice includes agreeing in advance what a strong answer looks like, scoring independently, and comparing notes afterwards. None of this is complicated, but it does require time that many managers say they do not have. Consistency matters more than cleverness: two assessors should reach similar conclusions.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Smaller firms face a particular difficulty. Designing, running and marking a realistic task costs money, and a business with a handful of employees may not have anyone free to do it. Some have joined forces with local colleges or industry groups to share the burden, while others use standardised tests bought from specialist providers. The risk is that a cheaper test drifts away from the actual demands of the job. A test borrowed from another industry may measure skills the job never requires.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: Assessment can also be gamed. Once candidates know what a test involves, coaching services appear, and the results start to measure preparation rather than ability. Companies defend themselves by changing tasks regularly and by observing how people work, not only what they produce. A candidate who has rehearsed an answer may still struggle when asked to explain a decision or to respond to an unexpected change. Honesty about the limits of testing is part of a credible process.

paragraphs.label: I
paragraphs.text: Degrees have not become irrelevant, but their role is shifting. A qualification still signals persistence and a certain level of knowledge, yet it is increasingly treated as one piece of evidence among several. In fields where the technology changes quickly, a portfolio of recent work may say more than a certificate earned years ago. Employers who insist on a degree in such fields risk excluding exactly the people who keep their skills current. What a candidate has built recently may matter more than what they studied years ago.

paragraphs.label: J
paragraphs.text: The hardest abilities to assess are the ones that matter most in teams: listening, negotiating and noticing when a colleague is struggling. A written exercise cannot easily capture them, and a group task may reward loudness. The best employers combine methods, using tests for technical skill and structured conversations for behaviour, and they accept that no single instrument is decisive. Judgement remains part of hiring, however many tools are added. No method removes the need for judgement, only the need to rely on a single impression.

statements.text: Interviews tend to reward confidence and fluency instead of evidence of competence.
Tasks modelled on real duties reveal abilities that conversation cannot.
Assessment can open doors for candidates without conventional qualifications.
Unpaid tasks disadvantage people with limited time, so safeguards are needed.
Existing employees can be moved according to demonstrated ability rather than titles.
Evaluators must be trained and use consistent criteria to avoid personal bias.
Small employers may share or buy assessment tools, though relevance can suffer.
Predictable tests invite coaching, so results reveal preparation as much as ability.
A degree now counts as one signal among many, especially where skills date quickly.
Teamwork qualities resist simple testing, so firms combine several methods.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Roads and railways cut the landscape into pieces. For an animal that needs a large territory, a motorway is not a line on a map but an impassable wall. Populations on one side become isolated, and over time they lose the genetic variety that helps them survive disease and climate stress. Fragmentation is a quieter threat than hunting or pollution, yet it may be the one that empties a forest of its larger inhabitants. The damage is done not by a single road but by the network that grows around it.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Engineers have responded with structures that let animals cross without meeting traffic. The best known are wide bridges covered with soil and planted with shrubs, which deer and foxes use without appearing to notice the road beneath. Underpasses serve smaller species, and tunnels built for drainage can be adapted for amphibians. Design matters: an opening that looks dark and narrow may be avoided even when it is perfectly safe. A crossing that animals refuse to use is an expensive decoration.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The evidence that such crossings work comes from cameras, footprints and tracking collars. Recordings show badgers, wild cats and even insects using the same routes night after night. Where a crossing has been placed badly, the data show that too, which allows the design to be corrected. Monitoring is unglamorous, but it turns a hopeful construction project into a measurable one. Without it, nobody can say whether the money was well spent.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Money and politics are the obvious obstacles. A wildlife bridge can cost as much as a small road, and the benefit is hard to demonstrate within a single political term. Supporters therefore emphasise the benefits to people: fewer collisions, safer journeys and, in some places, a tourist attraction. When a crossing is framed as a road-safety measure rather than an act of charity towards animals, it attracts a broader coalition. A project with a human justification is harder for a council to cut.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Large mammals attract the attention, but the smaller travellers matter just as much. Frogs, newts and beetles need connected patches of habitat, and a single busy road can wipe out a local population. Culverts, hedges and strips of rough grass allow these species to move between ponds and meadows. Because they are cheap to build and quick to establish, such measures are often the first step in a larger plan. A modest pipe under a lane can be as useful as a famous bridge.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Planting is part of the design, not a decoration added later. A corridor lined with native shrubs offers food and shelter, while a strip of mown grass offers neither. Species that evolved together with local plants are more likely to use a route that contains them. Ecologists therefore advise using seeds from nearby sources and avoiding ornamental species that may spread into the surrounding countryside. What looks green on a plan is not necessarily what an animal needs.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Drivers gain from these projects as well. A deer that crosses safely at a bridge is a deer that does not appear suddenly in headlights, and the reduction in collisions is felt in insurance claims and hospital admissions. Road authorities increasingly count wildlife crossings as part of their safety budget rather than their environmental one. For the public, the appeal is simple: a dangerous stretch of road becomes slightly less dangerous. Safety is easier to sell than ecology.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: Maintenance is the part nobody photographs. Fences must be repaired, vegetation must be cut back, and drainage must be cleared, or the crossing slowly stops being used. A structure that is opened with speeches can become a trap if rubbish blocks the entrance. Long-term funding is therefore as important as the original design, and some projects now include a maintenance plan before construction begins. A bridge without a budget for upkeep is a temporary gesture.

paragraphs.label: I
paragraphs.text: Cities have their own version of the problem. Parks and gardens are often too small and too isolated to support much wildlife, but a network of green roofs, balconies and planted streets can act as stepping stones. A bee may travel from one window box to the next without crossing a desert of concrete. Small interventions, repeated across a neighbourhood, can add up to a habitat that a single park could never provide. The scale is different, but the principle is the same.

paragraphs.label: J
paragraphs.text: The scale of the challenge crosses boundaries. An animal does not stop at the edge of a county, and a corridor that ends at a border is only half a corridor. Successful programmes therefore involve several authorities, landowners and conservation groups working to a shared plan. Where coordination fails, money is spent on fragments that connect nothing, and the map of safe routes remains full of gaps. Nature does not read the administrative map. Nor does it wait for agreements to be signed.

statements.text: Isolated groups lose the variation they need to cope with disease and environmental change.
Crossings must be designed carefully, because animals avoid openings that feel unsafe.
Cameras and tracking show whether a crossing is used and how to improve it.
Presenting crossings as safety measures helps win support and funding.
Small creatures also need connections, and cheap culverts and hedges can help them.
Native planting is essential to make a corridor useful rather than merely green.
Fewer collisions bring financial and medical benefits that road authorities recognise.
Without continuing upkeep, a crossing can fall into disuse and even become harmful.
In cities, many small green features can combine into a usable network.
Corridors only work when neighbouring authorities and owners plan together.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Software now decides many small things in a working day. It drafts the rota, ranks applications, allocates deliveries and flags which invoices look unusual. Managers welcome these tools because they remove repetitive labour and produce consistent decisions. Employees notice them in different ways: a shift appears without negotiation, or a task arrives with a score attached. The result is that a system nobody voted for can shape the rhythm of a workplace. Over a year, such small adjustments amount to a new way of working.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: One concern is that the data used to train such systems carries the assumptions of the people who collected it. If past hiring favoured a particular kind of candidate, a model taught on those decisions will reproduce the pattern while appearing neutral. The danger is subtle, because the output looks like arithmetic rather than opinion. Firms that audit their models sometimes discover that a variable they never considered relevant is doing most of the work. An unfair rule is hardest to challenge when it arrives as a number.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: There are clear benefits. Scheduling software can match staff to demand more fairly than a manager balancing favours and grudges, and it can give workers earlier notice of their hours. Administrative tools free people from paperwork that nobody enjoys. When the rules are visible, an employee can check why a decision was made instead of guessing. Used well, a system can make a workplace more predictable, not less. The difference lies in whether people can see the logic behind the schedule.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Transparency is the heart of the matter. Workers are entitled to know what information is collected about them, how it is used and who can see it. A system that watches keystrokes or tracks location may be justified in one job and intrusive in another. Good practice means explaining the purpose, limiting the data collected and allowing an independent check. Without those safeguards, monitoring becomes a source of suspicion rather than a tool for improvement. Trust is easier to keep than to rebuild.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The right to a human review matters when a decision goes wrong. A worker who is denied a promotion by an algorithm should be able to ask a person to explain and reconsider. Appeals are slow and costly, which is exactly why some employers skip them, but a system with no route to challenge invites resentment. A rule that cannot be questioned is experienced as unfair even when it happens to be correct. The possibility of appeal also keeps the system's designers careful.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The technology also changes what workers need to know. Staff are asked to interpret dashboards, correct bad data and recognise when a recommendation is nonsense. These are new skills, and they are not evenly distributed. Older employees and those in routine roles may need training that employers are reluctant to fund. A workplace that adopts a system without teaching people to use it has simply moved the difficulty from the manager's desk to the shop floor. The tool is only as good as the person reading it.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Metrics have a way of becoming targets. When performance is measured by the number of items processed, employees may process more items and care less about quality. When a system rewards speed, the quickest way to satisfy it is not always the best way to serve a customer. Managers who understand this use scores as one source of evidence rather than as a verdict, and they watch for the behaviour that measurement produces. A number that is trusted blindly will eventually be gamed.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: Collective bargaining has started to catch up. Unions increasingly ask for clauses that cover the introduction of new systems, including consultation before installation, limits on monitoring and access to the data held about members. Employers sometimes resist, yet clear rules protect them as well, because a workforce that understands a change is more likely to cooperate with it. The alternative is a series of disputes that cost both sides time. Agreement in advance is cheaper than a grievance later.

paragraphs.label: I
paragraphs.text: The long-term question is what happens to autonomy. A system that tells a worker which task to do next may raise productivity, but it also removes the small decisions that make a job interesting. Over time, the skills involved in planning and prioritising may weaken from disuse. Some organisations deliberately leave room for judgement, treating the software as an adviser rather than a supervisor. That choice, more than any technical feature, determines whether a job becomes better or merely faster. Efficiency and skill are not the same thing.

paragraphs.label: J
paragraphs.text: None of this is inevitable. Tools are adopted through decisions, and decisions can be shaped. Employees who are consulted early can point out problems that designers never imagined, and managers who ask what a system is for may discover that it solves the wrong problem. The technology will keep changing; what matters is whether the people affected have a voice in how it enters their working lives. A tool that is discussed before it is installed is far less likely to be resented.

statements.text: Unrequested systems can quietly determine the pattern of a working day.
Models can inherit past prejudices yet appear objective because they look numerical.
Visible rules and fairer scheduling can make working conditions more predictable.
Employees should know what is collected about them and why, with data kept limited.
Being able to appeal to a person is essential when an automated decision is wrong.
New tools demand new competences, and training is often neglected.
Measuring performance changes behaviour, so scores should inform rather than decide.
Unions are negotiating over consultation, monitoring limits and data access.
Removing small choices may erode skills and make work less satisfying.
The outcome depends on whether affected workers help decide how tools are introduced.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For a generation, the expected route out of school was a degree. Young people were told that university would open doors, and many took on debt to walk through them. The calculation is now less certain. Graduates compete for a limited number of entry-level roles, while skilled trades report shortages of people who can actually do the work. Families that once dismissed vocational training are beginning to ask whether a different path might be safer. The question is no longer whether university is good, but whether it is the only respectable choice.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: An apprenticeship combines both halves of the equation. The apprentice is employed, paid and taught on the job, while also studying part-time for a qualification. Because the training happens where the work happens, the learner sees the consequences of a mistake and the reason for a technique. The wage is modest, but it arrives from the first month, which changes the arithmetic for anyone who cannot afford to study unpaid. Learning and earning, once treated as opposites, happen at the same time.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Employers have their own reasons to value the model. A person trained inside a company learns its equipment, its standards and its customers, and is likely to stay. Replacing an experienced worker is expensive, and a home-grown apprentice is a way of filling a gap that the job market cannot supply. Firms that run good schemes describe them as an investment in the future rather than a cost to be minimised. Loyalty, they argue, is built in the first year and lost in the last.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The image problem has not disappeared. Many parents still associate apprenticeships with low status and limited prospects, and some schools steer able pupils towards university because it reflects well on the school. Careers advice can be patchy, and a teenager may hear about apprenticeships only from a leaflet. Changing this requires visible examples of people who started on the workshop floor and ended up running the business. Status follows success, and success needs to be shown.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Quality varies enormously. A well-run scheme rotates an apprentice through different departments, provides a mentor and links college study to real tasks. A poor one uses the label to hire cheap labour and teaches little beyond a single repetitive job. Because the word covers both, an applicant needs to ask careful questions about what the training will include, who will supervise it and what happened to previous apprentices. A title on a contract is not the same thing as training.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Mentoring is often the difference between a scheme that works and one that quietly fails. A young person entering a workplace needs someone to explain the unwritten rules, to correct a mistake without humiliation and to notice when confidence is slipping. Good mentors are not always the most technically expert; they are the ones who remember what it felt like to be new. Firms that treat mentoring as an extra duty tend to lose the people they trained. Time given to a beginner is rarely wasted.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Apprenticeships are no longer only for school leavers. Adults who spent years in one industry and now face a changing market can use the same structure to retrain, often with family commitments that make full-time study impossible. Employers gain maturity and reliability, while the learner gains a recognised qualification without abandoning paid work. The model fits an economy in which careers are less likely to follow a single straight line. A person can begin again without starting from nothing.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: Small businesses find the system harder to use. Taking on an apprentice means time for supervision, paperwork and contact with a college, and a firm with few staff may not be able to spare any of it. Group training schemes, where several employers share a trainer, help to spread the burden. Without such support, the firms that most need skilled workers are the least able to create them. The smallest businesses are often the best teachers and the least able to prove it.

paragraphs.label: I
paragraphs.text: Partnerships with colleges make the academic side work. A trainer who visits the workplace can adjust the syllabus to the tasks the apprentice actually performs, and a college can supply equipment that no single employer could justify buying. The arrangement fails when the two sides do not talk, leaving apprentices to study material that never appears in their daily work. Regular contact between tutor and supervisor is the practical fix. A course that ignores the workshop teaches half a trade.

paragraphs.label: J
paragraphs.text: Success is usually measured by completion. An apprentice who leaves before the end represents wasted money and a damaged expectation, so schemes track progress and intervene early when someone is struggling. Completion alone is not enough, however: the real test is whether the person is still using the skill years later, and whether the employer would take on another apprentice tomorrow. A programme that produces certificates but not confidence has missed the point. Numbers tell you who finished, not who stayed.

statements.text: Rising costs and uncertain graduate prospects make vocational routes look safer.
Apprentices earn while learning, which matters for those who cannot study unpaid.
Firms value workers shaped by their own standards because such people tend to stay.
The low-status image persists, partly because schools and advisers favour university.
Applicants should investigate what training a scheme really provides.
A mentor who remembers being new can keep a trainee from dropping out.
The model now serves adults changing careers, not only young school leavers.
Shared training arrangements help small firms that cannot supervise alone.
Colleges and workplaces must communicate so that study matches the job.
Completion rates matter, but lasting use of the skill is the truer test.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: A shelf holding six kinds of jam feels generous; a shelf holding sixty feels exhausting. The same shopper who enjoys comparing two options may freeze in front of twenty. Researchers describe the effect as choice overload, and the pattern is easy to recognise in daily life. A restaurant with an enormous menu can leave diners anxious that they have ordered the wrong thing, while a short menu often produces a happier table. Variety promises freedom but can deliver paralysis. The feeling is common enough to have a name.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Part of the difficulty is the effort of comparison. Each additional option must be examined, weighed against the others and remembered long enough to make a decision. That work is invisible but real, and it competes with everything else demanding attention. By the end of a day full of small decisions, the mind is tired in a way that sleep does not immediately fix, which is why a complicated choice at night is often postponed. The cost of choosing is paid in energy, not money.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Businesses have learned to use this fatigue. A default option, presented as the normal or recommended choice, saves the customer the trouble of deciding. Defaults are powerful because most people accept them, and they can be used well or badly. A pension scheme that enrols employees automatically may help them save, while a preselected expensive add-on exploits the same tendency for someone else's benefit. The same mechanism can serve the customer or the seller. The nudge is invisible unless someone points it out.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The opposite problem is just as real. When there are too few options, people feel trapped and resentful. A shop that stocks only one brand of coffee offers nothing to someone who dislikes it, and a service with a single plan forces customers into a shape that may not fit. The useful range seems to lie in the middle: enough variety to match different needs, but not so much that the choosing becomes the task. Too little choice is a cage; too much is a maze.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Online filters have changed the arithmetic. Good search tools let a buyer narrow a vast catalogue to a handful of plausible items, which restores the feeling of a manageable shelf. The quality of the filter matters more than the size of the catalogue. A site that ranks results by the seller's interests rather than the buyer's needs simply moves the confusion one step later. Better sorting can rescue a huge range; worse sorting can ruin a small one.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Some firms have responded by cutting their ranges. A restaurant that reduces its dishes serves food faster and wastes less, and a clothing brand with fewer designs can predict demand more accurately. Customers sometimes mourn a lost favourite, but many report that ordering became easier and mistakes rarer. The saving is not only financial: the staff also spend less time explaining options nobody wanted. A shorter list can be a form of respect. Waste falls, and so does the time spent explaining.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Regret is the companion of choice. Every option that is taken leaves others behind, and a person who has compared twenty possibilities can imagine the nineteen alternatives more vividly than someone who saw only two. This is why a crowded market can produce less satisfaction even when the chosen item is objectively better. The mind compares against what it almost had. Satisfaction depends as much on imagination as on the object itself.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: Time is the hidden cost. Researching a purchase, reading reviews, comparing prices and asking friends all consume hours that cannot be spent elsewhere. For a small decision the cost is trivial, but for a large one the research may grow until it outweighs the benefit of choosing well. Some people respond by setting a limit in advance: they will consider three options and then decide. A decision given a boundary is easier to make and easier to accept.

paragraphs.label: I
paragraphs.text: Personality plays a part. Some shoppers enjoy the search and treat comparison as a hobby, while others find it draining and prefer to decide quickly. The same wide selection that delights one customer irritates another. Sellers who assume that more choice always attracts more buyers may be ignoring the substantial group that pays for simplicity, and who will pay a premium to avoid a decision. Variety is a benefit to some and a tax on others.

paragraphs.label: J
paragraphs.text: The practical lesson is not to avoid choice but to structure it. Deciding what matters before looking, ignoring options that fail a basic test and accepting a good enough result can all reduce the burden. The aim is a decision that can be defended and then forgotten, rather than one that is revisited every time a new alternative appears. Good choosing is a skill, and like any skill it improves with a method. Freedom works best inside a frame.

statements.text: A very large set of options can make people uneasy instead of satisfied.
Comparing alternatives uses effort that adds to the day's mental fatigue.
Defaults exploit the wish to avoid deciding and may serve either side.
Too little variety also frustrates people, so a middle range works best.
Effective filters, not catalogue size, restore a sense of control.
Cutting ranges can make ordering simpler and operations more efficient.
Extensive comparison sharpens awareness of the options that were given up.
Research can consume more time than a decision is worth, so some set limits.
Attraction to variety differs between people, and simplicity can command a premium.
The answer is to organise the decision, not to escape it.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: When a new term begins, most students have the same worries: where to sit, which teachers to avoid and how to find friends. A club can answer all three. Members meet regularly, learn names quickly and share a task that gives them something to talk about. The friendships that form in a drama group or a chess club often outlast those made in class, because they grow from a shared interest rather than from sitting near each other. A common purpose is a good introduction. It is easier to talk to someone who is already doing the same thing.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Clubs also teach time management. A student who plays in the school band and studies for exams must decide what to do each evening and what to leave until tomorrow. That sounds like pressure, and sometimes it is, but it is also practice for adult life. Members usually discover that a busy week arranged well leaves more free time than an empty week that drifts. Planning is a habit, and a club gives it a reason. The skill is not the activity but the planning around it.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Many students join a club without knowing what they want. That is the point. A science club may reveal a taste for experiments; a debating society may show that an argument can be enjoyable. Trying an activity for a term is a cheap way to find out what one likes, and it is much less costly than choosing a university course on a guess. Curiosity is a better guide than a plan made too early. A term is short enough to be safe and long enough to be useful.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Clubs also give students a chance to lead. A treasurer, a secretary or a team captain learns to keep records, speak to adults and make decisions that affect other people. These roles are rarely offered in ordinary lessons. A student who has organised a charity collection or a school concert has evidence of responsibility that no examination can provide. Leadership, like any skill, is learned by doing it badly at first. Mistakes are cheaper here than in a first job.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Speaking in front of others becomes easier with practice. A member who has presented a report to fifteen classmates is less frightened by a job interview later. Clubs are forgiving places to make mistakes: the audience already knows the speaker and expects imperfection. Confidence grows from small successes rather than from a single lucky performance. A nervous first attempt is part of the training, not a verdict on talent. Practice, not perfection, is the aim of the first term.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Teachers can help, but they should not take over. A supportive teacher may find a room, explain the school's rules and suggest a sensible budget, while leaving the ideas to students. Clubs that depend entirely on one member of staff tend to collapse when that teacher changes school. The healthier pattern is a partnership in which adults advise and students decide. Help that creates dependence is not really help. Advice is welcome; a takeover is not.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: If no suitable club exists, students can start one. The process is usually less difficult than it appears: find a teacher willing to supervise, write a short plan, and ask for the use of a classroom once a week. Schools often welcome new groups because they improve the atmosphere. The first term is the hardest part, and a club needs only a few committed members to survive it. Every large club began with a small meeting. A notice board and a first meeting are enough to begin.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: Attendance is a commitment to other people. Members who leave early or arrive unprepared make the work heavier for everyone else, and a performance or a competition depends on everyone turning up. Learning to be reliable in a small group is a lesson that is difficult to teach in a classroom, and it is one that members remember long after they forget the club's name. Reliability is a habit that travels beyond school. Being counted on is a quiet kind of reward.

paragraphs.label: I
paragraphs.text: Some clubs serve the wider community. A group that visits a care home, collects food for a local charity or plants trees in a park teaches students that their time has value beyond school. The work is often simple, but it changes how members see their neighbourhood. It also looks good on applications, though that should not be the main reason for doing it. Service is most useful when nobody is counting the credit. The effort matters more than the size of the gesture.

paragraphs.label: J
paragraphs.text: Parents sometimes worry about cost. Uniforms, instruments and trips can be expensive, and not every family can pay. Most schools have funds or second-hand equipment, and a club that depends on money tends to attract only the students who have it. The best clubs are the ones that ask for enthusiasm first and money second. A group that welcomes everyone is also a better place to learn. A small contribution from many is better than a large one from few.

statements.text: Clubs help students make friends through shared interests rather than proximity.
Balancing activities with study teaches planning that carries into adulthood.
A term in a club is a low-cost way of discovering what one enjoys.
Roles such as treasurer or captain build skills that exams do not measure.
Presenting to a familiar audience makes later formal speaking less alarming.
Adults should guide without controlling, since a club depends on students.
Starting a group is manageable with a teacher's support and a simple plan.
Reliability matters because others depend on each member's contribution.
Service work gives students a sense that their time helps the wider community.
Cost should not decide who can join, so clubs should offer help.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: The first hour is the hardest. Without a screen to fill it, the morning feels strangely long, and the hand reaches for a phone that is not there. Most people describe the same set of feelings: restlessness, then boredom, then a kind of quiet. By the second hour the silence stops feeling like a problem and starts feeling like space. The discomfort is shorter than most people expect. Most people find the fear passes faster than they expected.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Time behaves differently without a screen. A walk that once seemed short now passes slowly enough to notice gardens, doorways and birds. Small tasks take as long as they take, instead of being squeezed between one message and the next. People report that the day feels longer, and not in a bad way: there is room in it for things that usually get postponed. Slowness, for once, is not a failure. A slow day is not an empty one.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Sleep often improves. Looking at a bright screen late in the evening keeps the mind alert and pushes bedtime later, so a weekend without screens often produces earlier nights. Waking without a phone is also different: instead of starting the day with other people's news, a person has a few minutes of their own thoughts. Many say that those minutes are the ones they miss most on Monday. Rest begins before the head touches the pillow. A screen-free evening is a small gift to the next morning.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Conversations change. Without a device on the table, family members talk for longer and interrupt less, and a meal can last an hour without anyone reaching for an update. There are silences, but they are not unpleasant. Several families report that the most interesting conversations happened during the gaps, when nobody had anything to fill. Attention is a form of generosity, and it can be felt. A shared silence can be comfortable when nobody is escaping into a screen.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Outdoor activity becomes the obvious alternative. A bike ride, a game in the park or a walk to the shops replaces the hours that would have been spent scrolling. None of this needs to be organised or expensive; the point is that the body is moving and the mind is following it. Even weeding a garden can feel satisfying when it is done without a podcast in the ears. Movement offers the mind something to hold. The body rarely needs encouragement when the phone is away.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Planning ahead helps. A weekend of nothing but prohibition is likely to end in a relapse, so experienced people prepare a few alternatives: a book, a recipe, a friend to visit or a job that has been waiting. The plan should be flexible. The aim is not to fill every hour but to have an obvious next thing to do when the hand reaches for the phone. A little preparation protects a good intention. Without a plan, the phone wins by default.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The experiment is not a permanent rule. Few people want to abandon their devices completely, and there are good reasons to answer a message from a relative or check the weather. The useful conclusion is that screens are a choice rather than a reflex. A person who has spent a weekend without them usually returns with a clearer sense of when a device helps and when it merely fills a gap. The point is control, not abstinence. A tool used on purpose is different from a tool used out of habit.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: Social pressure is real. Friends expect quick replies, and a silence can seem rude. It helps to tell people in advance that replies will be slow, and to leave one channel open for emergencies. Most friends are understanding once they know the reason, and some are curious enough to try a quiet weekend themselves. A boundary explained is usually a boundary respected. Silence surprises people only when it is unexplained. A short honest message prevents most misunderstandings.

paragraphs.label: I
paragraphs.text: Children and teenagers react differently. Younger children may enjoy the novelty at first and then complain of boredom, which is often the beginning of play. Teenagers may feel cut off from friends and need a compromise that keeps some contact while limiting the endless scroll. A family rule works better when it is discussed than when it is announced. The young are quick to detect a rule that adults do not follow themselves. Consistency in adults matters more than strictness.

paragraphs.label: J
paragraphs.text: The habit rarely lasts exactly as planned, and that is fine. Most people return to their phones by Monday, but they keep one small change: a phone left in another room at night, a screen-free meal or a walk without headphones. A weekend is too short to transform a life, but it is long enough to show that the life can be arranged differently. Small changes survive where grand resolutions do not. A habit kept is worth more than a rule broken.

statements.text: The initial discomfort gives way to a sense of openness.
Without a screen, everyday life unfolds at a pace that reveals small details.
Fewer late-night screens and calmer mornings improve rest.
Meals without devices last longer and allow real exchange.
Physical activity naturally takes the place of scrolling.
Preparing flexible options prevents the attempt from collapsing.
The weekend shows that devices should be used deliberately, not automatically.
Telling friends beforehand makes the break easier to sustain.
Younger family members need different arrangements and discussion.
Small lasting changes are a more realistic outcome than total abstinence.

items.title: Translation 翻译
items.paperTitle: 2024年12月大学英语四级（模拟节选）
items.prompt: 中国的移动支付近年来发展迅速。如今，无论是在城市还是乡村，人们只需用手机扫一扫二维码，就可以购买商品、乘坐公交，甚至缴纳水电费。移动支付不仅节省了时间，还减少了人们对现金的依赖。许多外国游客对此感到惊讶，认为这是中国日常生活中最方便的发明之一。
items.reference: Mobile payment has developed rapidly in China in recent years. Today, whether in cities or in the countryside, people can simply scan a QR code with their mobile phones to buy goods, take a bus, or even pay their water and electricity bills. Mobile payment not only saves time but also reduces people's reliance on cash. Many foreign visitors are surprised by it and regard it as one of the most convenient inventions in daily life in China.

items.title: Translation 翻译
items.paperTitle: 大学英语四级标准模拟卷 01
items.prompt: 中国是茶的故乡，饮茶的历史已有数千年。茶不仅是一种饮品，也是一种生活方式。客人来访时，主人通常会先奉上一杯热茶，以表示欢迎与尊重。不同地区的人们喜爱不同的茶：南方人偏爱绿茶，北方人则更常喝花茶。近年来，越来越多的年轻人开始学习茶艺，茶馆也成了朋友聚会的好去处。茶文化强调平静与分享，这或许正是它在快节奏的现代生活中依然受欢迎的原因。
items.reference: China is the home of tea, and the history of tea drinking there goes back thousands of years. Tea is not only a drink but also a way of life. When guests visit, the host usually offers them a cup of hot tea first as a sign of welcome and respect. People in different regions prefer different kinds of tea: those in the south favour green tea, while those in the north more often drink scented tea. In recent years, more and more young people have begun to learn the art of tea making, and tea houses have become popular places for friends to meet. Tea culture stresses calmness and sharing, which may explain why it is still welcome in the fast pace of modern life.

items.title: Translation 翻译
items.paperTitle: 大学英语四级标准模拟卷 02
items.prompt: 中国高铁的发展速度令世界瞩目。如今，高铁网络连接了全国大多数大中城市，从北京到上海只需四个多小时。高铁不仅缩短了城市之间的时间距离，也改变了人们的生活方式：有人乘高铁上下班，有人周末去另一座城市看展览。与飞机相比，高铁车站通常离市区更近，乘车手续也更简便。许多外国游客把乘坐中国高铁列为旅行中难忘的体验。高铁还带动了沿线小城市的发展，使人才和资源流动更加便利。
items.reference: The development of China's high-speed railway has attracted worldwide attention. Today the network connects most large and medium-sized cities in the country, and the journey from Beijing to Shanghai takes only a little over four hours. High-speed trains have not only shortened the travel time between cities but also changed the way people live: some people commute by high-speed train, and others travel to another city for an exhibition at the weekend. Compared with planes, high-speed railway stations are usually closer to city centres and the boarding procedures are simpler. Many foreign visitors regard a ride on a Chinese high-speed train as an unforgettable experience of their trip. The railways have also boosted the development of smaller cities along the lines, making it easier for talent and resources to flow.

items.title: Translation 翻译
items.paperTitle: 大学英语四级标准模拟卷 03
items.prompt: “绿水青山就是金山银山”这一理念如今被越来越多的中国人所熟悉。它提醒我们，保护环境与发展经济并不矛盾。近年来，许多地方通过植树造林、治理河流和建设公园，让曾经污染的矿区变成了旅游景点。当地居民靠经营民宿和出售农产品增加了收入，也更加珍惜身边的环境。绿色发展意味着节约资源、减少浪费，把干净的空气和水留给下一代。这不仅是政府的责任，也需要每个人从日常生活做起。
items.reference: The idea that green mountains and clear waters are as valuable as gold and silver is now familiar to more and more Chinese people. It reminds us that protecting the environment and developing the economy do not contradict each other. In recent years, many places have turned polluted mining areas into tourist attractions by planting trees, cleaning up rivers and building parks. Local residents have earned more by running guesthouses and selling farm products, and they value the environment around them even more. Green development means saving resources, reducing waste and leaving clean air and water to the next generation. This is not only the responsibility of the government; it also requires each of us to start with our daily lives.

items.title: Translation 翻译
items.paperTitle: 大学英语四级标准模拟卷 04
items.prompt: 敦煌莫高窟位于中国西北的沙漠之中，是世界上规模最大的佛教艺术宝库之一。自公元四世纪起，人们在洞窟中绘制壁画、塑造佛像，历经千余年，留下了大量珍贵的艺术品。这些洞窟不仅记录了佛教在中国的传播，也反映了古代丝绸之路上的商贸往来与文化交流。近年来，研究人员利用数字技术对壁画进行高精度拍摄，建立了完整的图像档案，使这些脆弱的艺术珍品得以长久保存，也让世界各地的人们可以在线欣赏它们的美丽。
items.reference: The Mogao Caves in Dunhuang, located in the desert of northwest China, are one of the largest treasure houses of Buddhist art in the world. Since the fourth century, people have painted murals and made statues of Buddha in these caves. Over more than a thousand years they left behind a great number of precious works of art. The caves not only record how Buddhism spread in China but also reflect the trade and cultural exchanges along the ancient Silk Road. In recent years, researchers have used digital technology to photograph the murals at high resolution and have built a complete image archive. As a result, these fragile treasures can be preserved for a long time, and people all over the world can enjoy their beauty online.

items.title: Translation 翻译
items.paperTitle: 大学英语四级标准模拟卷 05
items.prompt: 春节是中国最重要的传统节日。每到农历新年，人们会提前几周打扫房屋、贴春联、准备丰盛的年夜饭。除夕之夜，全家人尽量聚在一起吃团圆饭，长辈还会给孩子压岁钱。许多地方还保留着放鞭炮、舞龙舞狮的习俗，寓意辞旧迎新、祈求来年吉祥。如今，虽然城市里对燃放烟花有严格限制，但人们通过视频通话、电子红包等方式，同样传递着对亲友的祝福和对新年的期盼。
items.reference: The Spring Festival is the most important traditional festival in China. As the lunar new year approaches, people clean their houses, put up spring couplets and prepare a rich dinner several weeks in advance. On New Year's Eve, the whole family tries to get together for a reunion meal, and elders give children lucky money. In many places the old customs of setting off firecrackers and performing dragon and lion dances are still kept, which means saying goodbye to the old year and praying for good luck in the coming one. Today, although setting off fireworks is strictly limited in cities, people still send their good wishes and hopes for the new year to relatives and friends through video calls and electronic red envelopes.

items.title: Translation 翻译
items.paperTitle: 大学英语四级标准模拟卷 06
items.prompt: 丝绸之路是古代连接中国与中亚、欧洲的重要商路。两千多年前，商人们沿着这条道路，把中国的丝绸、茶叶和瓷器运往西方，也把葡萄、香料和音乐带回中国。丝绸之路不仅是一条贸易通道，更是一条文化交流之路。沿着它，佛教传入中国，中国的造纸术也传向世界。今天，这条古老的商路依然吸引着无数旅行者和学者，人们希望从中了解不同文明如何相互学习、共同发展。
items.reference: The Silk Road was an important trade route linking China with Central Asia and Europe in ancient times. More than two thousand years ago, traders carried Chinese silk, tea and porcelain to the West along this road, and brought grapes, spices and music back to China. The Silk Road was not only a trade route but also a road of cultural exchange. Along it, Buddhism spread into China, and Chinese paper-making techniques travelled to the rest of the world. Today this ancient route still attracts countless travellers and scholars, who hope to learn from it how different civilizations can learn from one another and develop together.

items.title: Translation 翻译
items.paperTitle: 大学英语四级标准模拟卷 07
items.prompt: 中国的移动支付已经成为日常生活中很普通的一部分。无论是在超市结账，还是在路边买一份早点，人们只要拿出手机扫一下二维码，几秒钟就能完成付款。这种方式不仅省去了排队找零的麻烦，也让许多小摊主不必准备大量现金。对游客来说，移动支付同样方便，他们可以在手机上绑定银行卡，用一部手机完成旅行中的大部分消费。不过，也有老人表示，自己不太会使用这些软件，希望商家仍然保留现金支付的选项。
items.reference: Mobile payment has become an ordinary part of daily life in China. Whether paying at a supermarket checkout or buying breakfast at a roadside stall, people only need to take out their phones and scan a QR code, and the payment is completed within seconds. This method not only saves the trouble of queuing and making change, but also means that many small stallholders no longer need to keep large amounts of cash. For visitors, mobile payment is convenient as well: they can link a bank card to their phone and use a single device for most of their spending during a trip. Some elderly people, however, say that they are not good at using these apps and hope that shops will still keep the option of paying in cash.

items.title: Translation 翻译
items.paperTitle: 大学英语四级标准模拟卷 08
items.prompt: 中医是中国传统医学的重要组成部分，它强调人体与自然环境的平衡。中医认为，人的健康取决于饮食、情绪、作息等因素是否协调，因此提出了许多日常养生的方法。例如，在寒冷的季节多吃温热的食物，在夏天注意补充水分；保持规律的作息，避免过度劳累。近年来，越来越多的年轻人开始关注中医养生，学习按摩和药膳。不过，专家提醒，养生方法应当根据个人体质选择，不能盲目照搬。
items.reference: Traditional Chinese medicine is an important part of China's traditional medical culture, and it stresses the balance between the human body and the natural environment. In its view, a person's health depends on whether diet, emotions and daily routines are in harmony, so many methods of everyday health care have been developed. For example, people are advised to eat warm food in cold seasons and to drink enough water in summer, and to keep regular hours and avoid overwork. In recent years, more and more young people have become interested in traditional health care and have started learning massage and medicinal dishes. Experts remind them, however, that such methods should be chosen according to individual constitution rather than copied blindly.

items.title: Translation 翻译
items.paperTitle: 大学英语四级标准模拟卷 09
items.prompt: 近年来，中国许多城市修建了绿道，把公园、河流和居民区连接起来。绿道两旁种满树木，设有步道和自行车道，市民可以在那里散步、跑步或骑行。这些绿色空间不仅改善了城市环境，也为邻里交往提供了场所。周末，常能看到父母带着孩子骑车，老人在树荫下聊天。专家认为，城市在建设绿道时，应当考虑不同人群的需要，并做好日常维护，让这些空间真正融入居民的生活。
items.reference: In recent years, many Chinese cities have built greenways that connect parks, rivers and residential areas. The greenways are lined with trees and provided with footpaths and cycle lanes, where citizens can walk, run or ride. These green spaces not only improve the urban environment but also offer places for neighbours to meet. At weekends, it is common to see parents cycling with their children and elderly people chatting in the shade of the trees. Experts believe that when building greenways, cities should take the needs of different groups into account and carry out regular maintenance, so that these spaces truly become part of residents' lives.

items.title: Translation 翻译
items.paperTitle: 大学英语四级标准模拟卷 10
items.prompt: 数字经济正成为中国经济增长的重要动力。随着5G网络的普及，人们可以在几秒钟内下载一部电影，偏远地区的病人也能通过视频接受城市医生的诊断。在工厂里，5G技术让机器之间的配合更加精确，生产效率明显提高。专家认为，数字技术不仅创造了新的产业，也改变了普通人的生活方式。未来，如何让更多人分享数字红利，将是一项重要的社会课题。
items.reference: The digital economy is becoming an important driver of China's economic growth. With the spread of 5G networks, people can download a film within seconds, and patients in remote areas can be diagnosed by city doctors through video calls. In factories, 5G technology allows machines to work together more precisely, and production efficiency has improved markedly. Experts believe that digital technology has not only created new industries but also changed the way ordinary people live. In the future, how to let more people share the benefits of the digital economy will be an important social question.

items.title: Translation 翻译
items.paperTitle: 2023年12月大学英语四级真题风格卷（原创题面）
items.prompt: 元旦前夕，学校礼堂里举行了一场联欢晚会。师生们自己编排节目，有合唱、舞蹈，也有小品和乐器演奏。晚会开始时，校长发表了简短的新年致辞，随后屏幕上播放了一年来校园生活的照片。最受欢迎的环节是抽奖，幸运的同学得到了书和文具。午夜钟声敲响时，全场一起倒数，互相祝福新年快乐。这样的晚会不仅让大家放松，也让师生之间的关系更加亲近。
items.reference: On New Year's Eve, a gala was held in the school hall. Teachers and students put on the performances themselves, including a chorus, dances, short plays and instrumental music. At the beginning of the gala, the headmaster gave a short New Year speech, and then photos of campus life over the past year were shown on the screen. The most popular part was the lucky draw, in which lucky students received books and stationery. When the clock struck midnight, everyone counted down together and wished each other a happy New Year. Such a gala not only helps people relax but also brings teachers and students closer to each other.

items.title: Translation 翻译
items.paperTitle: 2024年6月大学英语四级真题风格卷（原创题面）
items.prompt: 农历是中国传统的历法，已有几千年的历史。它根据月亮的变化来划分月份，同时通过设置闰月来适应四季的更替。对中国农民来说，农历指导着播种和收获；对普通人来说，春节、端午节和中秋节等传统节日都按照农历计算。即使在今天，许多家庭仍然会在农历生日那天吃长寿面，也会在春节前贴上红色的春联。农历不仅是一种记时的方法，也承载着中国人的文化记忆。
items.reference: The lunar calendar is a traditional Chinese calendar with a history of several thousand years. It divides the months according to the changes of the moon, and at the same time adjusts to the change of the four seasons by adding leap months. For Chinese farmers, the lunar calendar guides sowing and harvesting; for ordinary people, traditional festivals such as the Spring Festival, the Dragon Boat Festival and the Mid-Autumn Festival are all calculated according to the lunar calendar. Even today, many families still eat long noodles on their lunar birthdays and put up red couplets before the Spring Festival. The lunar calendar is not only a way of keeping time but also carries the cultural memory of the Chinese people.

items.title: Translation 翻译
items.paperTitle: 2024年12月大学英语四级真题风格卷（原创题面）
items.prompt: 近年来，中国新能源汽车产业发展迅速。越来越多的人选择购买电动汽车，既因为充电比加油便宜，也因为人们更加关注空气质量和环境保护。在城市里，充电桩已经出现在停车场、商场和居民小区中。中国企业还在电池技术和智能驾驶方面不断取得突破，一些品牌的汽车已经出口到许多国家。不过，行业也面临充电设施分布不均、电池回收等问题。专家认为，只有持续创新并完善相关服务，新能源汽车才能走进更多家庭。
items.reference: In recent years, China's new energy vehicle industry has developed rapidly. More and more people choose to buy electric cars, partly because charging is cheaper than buying petrol, and partly because they pay greater attention to air quality and environmental protection. In cities, charging piles have appeared in car parks, shopping malls and residential communities. Chinese companies have also kept making breakthroughs in battery technology and intelligent driving, and cars from some brands have already been exported to many countries. However, the industry still faces problems such as the uneven distribution of charging facilities and the recycling of used batteries. Experts believe that only by continuing to innovate and improving related services can new energy vehicles truly reach more families.

items.title: Translation 翻译
items.paperTitle: 2025年6月大学英语四级真题风格卷（原创题面）
items.prompt: 中国园林有着悠久的历史，是中华文化的重要组成部分。与中国北方的皇家园林不同，江南的私家园林往往面积不大，却通过假山、水池、花木和曲折的回廊营造出变化丰富的空间。设计者讲究「借景」和「步移景异」，让游人在有限的地方感受到自然的意趣。园林中的亭台楼阁不仅是休息之处，也常被用来读书、作画和会友。今天，许多古典园林已成为著名的旅游景点，吸引着世界各地的游客。保护这些园林，就是保护一种独特的生活方式和审美传统。
items.reference: Chinese gardens have a long history and form an important part of Chinese culture. Unlike the royal gardens of northern China, private gardens in the region south of the Yangtze are often small in size, yet they create a rich variety of space through rockeries, ponds, flowers and trees, and winding corridors. Their designers paid great attention to borrowing views from the surroundings and to making the scenery change with every step, so that visitors can feel the charm of nature within a limited area. The pavilions and towers in these gardens were not only places to rest, but also places to read, paint and meet friends. Today many classical gardens have become famous tourist attractions that draw visitors from all over the world. To protect them is to protect a distinctive way of life and a tradition of beauty.

items.title: Translation 翻译
items.paperTitle: 2025年12月大学英语四级真题风格卷（原创题面）
items.prompt: 近年来，城市漫步在年轻人中越来越受欢迎。与赶路式的旅游不同，它强调放慢脚步，随意走进老街区、小巷和公园，感受城市的历史与日常生活。一些城市还设计了主题漫步路线。有人认为这只是社交网络上的风潮，但它确实让人们重新认识了身边的城市，也让一些老街区获得新的活力。专家建议，城市漫步应尊重居民生活，不要打扰社区安宁。
items.reference: In recent years, city walking has become increasingly popular among young people. Unlike travel that is all about rushing from one sight to another, it encourages people to slow down, wander into old neighbourhoods, narrow lanes and parks, and feel the history and daily life of a city as they walk. Some cities have designed themed walking routes.
